# About Stephen P. Pryor, CPA

## Identity
Stephen P. Pryor, CPA is a CPA firm founded in 1990 by Stephen P. Pryor, based in Port Chester, New York. The firm serves the great majority of its clients in Westchester County, with additional clients in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Asbury Park, New Jersey, and clients across New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Florida.

The firm's team is service and relationship driven. Stephen P. Pryor manages the firm and client relations with expertise in taxation. Shawn Wilson, Managing Director, brings over a decade of experience with high net worth individuals and business clients in construction, hospitality, and rental real estate. Nicholas Vergara, Senior Manager, handles compliance filings for payroll, sales tax, business income tax, and financial statements for retail, construction, real estate, and hospitality clients. Denise Romano, Senior Accountant, assists with personal and corporate tax returns, financial statements, payroll, and sales tax. Nancy Pryor, Office Director, has supported the firm since it opened in 1990. Kelly Pryor coordinates projects, billing, and individual tax return workflow. Angelique Lecaj handles payroll, sales tax, and income tax filings while pursuing her CPA license. Francis Moran serves as Senior Manager, and Allison Jubelirer supports senior accountants with data entry and records.

The firm's mission is built on service and relationships: it accommodates and takes care of clients, listens closely to address their issues and stresses, and learns each client's internal systems during onboarding.

## Positioning & Differentiation
Stephen P. Pryor, CPA positions itself with the tagline: "You run your business. We'll run your numbers." Its positioning statement describes the firm as a hands-on advisory partner that listens closely and brings deep expertise in construction, real estate, and hospitality, with a specialty in bars and pubs.

The firm differentiates itself through bundled services for a fixed monthly fee, a secure online platform for real-time financial data, personalized year-round support, and deep industry-specific expertise in construction, real estate, and hospitality.

Ideal clients include construction businesses, real estate businesses, hospitality businesses, service-based businesses, and new business owners, typically in the 35 to 60 age range. Clients seek a trusted advisor they can rely on year-round, guidance and advice rather than compliance work alone, and someone who understands their business and proactively helps them make better financial decisions. Clients most often find the firm through referrals and online search.

Services span bookkeeping, tax preparation and planning, payroll, outsourced accounting, business foundation services for new business owners, audit protection, personal income tax, entity type analysis, accounting system setup, retirement plan analysis, and cash management.

## Industries Served

### Construction
The firm provides specialized construction accounting expertise, addressing pain points including inconsistent cash flow between project phases, job costing complexity and tracking profitability per project, payroll compliance for mixed workforces of W-2 employees and 1099 subcontractors, surprise tax bills from poor quarterly planning, and bonding and banking requirements that demand clean financials.

### Real Estate
The firm offers accounting and advisory support tailored to rental real estate clients, including cost segregation and like-kind exchanges under Section 1031. Pain points addressed include maximizing depreciation and identifying cost segregation opportunities, navigating 1031 exchanges without triggering unexpected tax liability, understanding passive activity loss rules and how they interact with other income, poor record-keeping across multiple properties, and confusion around entity structure for holding properties.

### Bars and Restaurants
The firm focuses on bars and pubs, not high-end restaurants, providing cash flow management and compliance support for bar and pub operators. Pain points addressed include thin margins with no visibility into where money is going, cash handling and tip reporting compliance, sales tax complexity across food, alcohol, and delivery, high payroll costs and turnover creating administrative burden, and a lack of financial reporting to support informed operational decisions.

### Individuals and Households
The firm provides individual tax clients with personal income tax preparation and year-round tax advice. Pain points addressed include being overwhelmed by tax complexity, especially with side income or investments, missed deductions from lack of year-round planning, anxiety around IRS notices or audit risk, tax confusion created by life changes such as marriage, divorce, inheritance, or home sale, and not having anyone to call when a financial question comes up mid-year.

## Industries we serve

### Construction
URL: /industries/construction

<!-- block: hero-split | variant: image-right -->

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: construction-job-site-review.jpg | alt: "Contractor and CPA reviewing project costs on a construction site" | query: "contractor accountant reviewing blueprints" -->
## A CPA firm that understands construction businesses

Construction is a cash business until it isn't. Money goes out for materials, labor, and permits long before a project bills out. If you're not tracking each job separately, you can look profitable on paper while the bank account tells a different story.

Stephen P. Pryor, CPA has worked with contractors, builders, and subcontractors across Port Chester and Westchester County long enough to know that construction accounting isn't really about ledgers. It's about knowing which job is making money and which one is quietly costing you.

Bookkeeping, payroll, tax, and advisory come bundled into one fixed monthly fee, so a phone call about a job cost question doesn't turn into a surprise invoice. One team learns your job costing system, your subcontractor list, and your crew, and stays with you as the work changes.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: construction-cash-flow-planning.jpg | alt: "Construction business owner reviewing cash flow reports and invoices" | query: "contractor reviewing financial reports office" -->
## The financial challenges construction companies face

Contractors don't lose money because they're bad at the work. They lose it because the accounting doesn't keep pace with how construction actually operates: draws, retainage, change orders, and crews moving between sites. Before we open a single ledger, we've usually already seen these problems play out on other job sites across Westchester County.

- Cash flow that swings hard between project phases, with big outlays up front and payment held until milestones or final completion
- Job costing that's tracked by feel instead of by phase, making it hard to know which contracts are actually profitable
- Payroll complications from union scales, prevailing wage requirements, certified payroll reporting, and crews split across multiple job sites
- Retainage and change orders that get lost in the shuffle, shrinking margins nobody notices until the project closes out
- Subcontractor payments and 1099 tracking that pile up at year end instead of getting handled as the work happens

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: job-costing-bookkeeping-review.jpg | alt: "Bookkeeper analyzing project cost reports for a construction company" | query: "bookkeeper reviewing project cost spreadsheet" -->
## Bookkeeping built around job costing and project profitability

Generic bookkeeping treats every expense the same. Construction bookkeeping has to answer a different question: is this specific job making money, right now, at this phase? Our [bookkeeping](/services/bookkeeping) service tracks costs by project and by phase, so labor, materials, subcontractor draws, and overhead all get coded to the job they belong to.

That means you can see a phase-by-phase profitability picture instead of waiting for a year-end report to tell you a job lost money three months after it closed. Bills get tracked, invoices go out on time, and the numbers stay current enough to actually inform a bid on the next job. When a contract runs over budget, you find out while there's still time to do something about it, not after the final draw.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: construction-crew-payroll-check.jpg | alt: "Construction crew reviewing payroll documents on a job site" | query: "construction crew reviewing paperwork job site" -->
## Payroll support for crews, subcontractors, and multi-site jobs

Construction payroll rarely looks like a standard nine-to-five payroll run. Crews split time across multiple job sites in a single week. Union scales and prevailing wage rates change the math from one contract to the next, and certified payroll reporting has to be right, because a mistake there can hold up a draw or trigger a compliance headache with a public project.

Our [payroll](/services/payroll) service is built to handle that complexity: multiple pay rates, job-site allocation, subcontractor payments, and the filings that come with them, processed accurately and on time. Crews get paid correctly, compliance paperwork gets filed, and you're not the one untangling a payroll report at 9pm before a certified payroll deadline.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: contractor-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Construction business owner and CPA discussing tax planning documents" | query: "small business owner meeting accountant tax" -->
## Tax planning and entity strategy for contractors

Tax season shouldn't be the first time you find out how the year actually went. Year-round [tax](/services/tax) planning means we're looking at your numbers throughout the year, not just in March, so estimated payments, equipment purchases, and entity decisions get made with the whole picture in view instead of a rear-view mirror.

As construction businesses grow, take on bigger contracts, or add partners, the right legal entity structure changes too. Our [entity type analysis](/what-we-do/entity-type-analysis) looks at how your business is set up today against where it's headed, covering the state and federal tax implications of S-corp, partnership, and LLC structures for contractors. Getting that structure right before a big contract year, not after, is usually where the real tax savings show up.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: contractor-mobile-financial-dashboard.jpg | alt: "Contractor checking financial dashboard on a laptop at a job site" | query: "contractor laptop financial dashboard site" -->
## Real-time visibility into your numbers

You shouldn't have to call the office to find out how a job is trending. Our secure online platform gives you real-time access to job costs, cash flow, and financial reports from the trailer, the truck, or the office, whenever you need a number, not just at month-end.

That kind of visibility matters most on active jobs, when a labor overrun or a material price spike needs a decision this week, not next quarter. Paired with [cash management](/what-we-do/cash-management) support, it means you're watching cash position and job profitability at the same time, instead of guessing at both.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: contractor-handshake-office-meeting.jpg | alt: "Construction business owner shaking hands with a CPA advisor" | query: "business handshake meeting professional office" -->
## Let's talk about your construction business

You already carry enough on a job site. Let Stephen P. Pryor, CPA carry the numbers: job costing, payroll, tax planning, and the entity structure that fits where your construction business is headed. Contractors across Port Chester, Westchester County, and beyond work with us because they'd rather spend their time on the next bid than the last invoice.

[Schedule a consultation](/contact) and let's talk about what your construction business actually needs from its accounting.

### Real Estate
URL: /industries/real-estate

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: real-estate-cpa-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA reviewing property portfolio documents with a real estate investor" | query: "real estate investor meeting accountant" -->
## A CPA firm that understands real estate investors and property owners

Owning rental property is a different kind of business. The numbers behind a four-unit building in Rye don't look like the numbers behind a retail shop or a construction crew, and a CPA who treats them the same way will miss things. Depreciation schedules, passive activity limits, entities layered across multiple properties: this is where a generalist practice starts to fall short.

Stephen P. Pryor, CPA works with landlords, investors, brokers, and property management companies across Port Chester and the rest of Westchester County, with clients also in Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Asbury Park, NJ. Stephen Pryor, CPA, Shawn Wilson, CPA, and Denise Romano, CPA bring real estate specifics into every conversation, not boilerplate advice pulled from a small business checklist. You get a firm that already knows what questions to ask about your portfolio before you finish explaining it.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: property-portfolio-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant analyzing rental property financial statements on laptop" | query: "accountant reviewing property financial documents" -->
## Solving the financial challenges unique to real estate

Most of the real estate owners who come to us are leaving money on the table somewhere, usually without knowing it. A cost segregation study that was never run. Depreciation that's being calculated the slow way instead of the strategic way. A 1031 exchange that got done but triggered a tax surprise nobody saw coming because a deadline or a like-kind detail got missed.

We look at the full picture of how a property or a portfolio is structured and taxed, then find where the strategy is underused.

- Maximizing depreciation through cost segregation studies and accelerated schedules
- Structuring 1031 exchanges correctly, with attention to timelines and reinvestment rules
- Reviewing passive activity classifications so losses aren't disallowed unexpectedly
- Coordinating entity structure with tax strategy across multi-property portfolios
- Catching sales tax and local filing obligations tied to property transactions

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: landlord-bookkeeping-review.jpg | alt: "Property manager and accountant reviewing rental income spreadsheets together" | query: "landlord reviewing rental property finances" -->
## Bookkeeping and accounting built for landlords and property portfolios

When rent comes in from six properties and expenses go out to a dozen vendors, spreadsheets stop being enough. Our bookkeeping service tracks rental income and expenses property by property, reconciles bank and escrow accounts, and keeps your books current instead of catching up every quarter.

Everything runs through a secure online platform, so you can check occupancy income, maintenance costs, or a single property's performance whenever you need to, not just when tax season rolls around. If a lender asks for current financials or a partner wants to see how a building is performing, the numbers are already there and already accurate.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: real-estate-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA discussing tax planning strategy with real estate investor at desk" | query: "tax planning meeting real estate client" -->
## Tax planning and preparation for real estate owners and investors

Real estate tax work doesn't end when the return gets filed. Passive activity rules, depreciation recapture, and multi-property gains and losses need to be modeled out before year-end, not discovered after. We build tax projections throughout the year so you know what a sale, a refinance, or a new acquisition will mean for your bill before it happens.

That includes year-round planning around depreciation strategy, entity-level tax positioning, and how income from different properties or partnerships flows through to your personal return. For real estate agents and brokers, we also handle self-employment tax planning and quarterly estimates so there are no surprises in April.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Choosing the right entity structure for your real estate holdings

Holding property in your own name, an LLC, or a series of LLCs changes both your liability exposure and your tax outcome, and the right answer depends on how many properties you own, how they're financed, and whether you're planning to sell, refinance, or hold long term. We walk through entity type analysis with real estate clients specifically, weighing single-member LLCs against multi-entity holding structures, S-corp elections for management companies, and how each option affects federal and New York state tax filings.

This isn't a one-time conversation. As a portfolio grows or a property gets refinanced, the structure that made sense at the start may need to change, and we revisit it as your holdings do.

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->

### Advisory as your portfolio scales
icon: ChartLine

Acquiring another property, refinancing, or bringing on a partner changes your financial picture. We provide advisory support that looks at the decision before you make it, not just the tax return after.

Vacancy gaps, capital improvements, and seasonal expenses hit differently across a multi-property portfolio. We help you see cash position across all your holdings so you're planning ahead instead of reacting.

## A CPA who understands the restaurant business

Running a bar or restaurant in Port Chester means thin margins, unpredictable weeks, and a hundred small decisions that add up fast. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA has spent years working with hospitality operators across Westchester County who need more than someone to file a return once a year.

Bars and pubs are a specific focus of this firm, not an afterthought. Food and beverage cost ratios, tip credit rules, seasonal staffing swings, and cash-heavy operations all require a different level of attention than a typical small business. Stephen and the team, including Shawn Wilson, CPA and Denise Romano, CPA, learn how your restaurant actually runs during onboarding, from your POS system to your vendor terms, so the numbers reflect reality from day one.

Clients from Port Chester to Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Asbury Park, NJ rely on this hands-on approach instead of a once-a-year check-in.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: restaurant-bookkeeping-daily-transactions.jpg | alt: "Bookkeeper organizing restaurant invoices and receipts at a desk" | query: "bookkeeper reviewing restaurant invoices" -->
## Bookkeeping built for daily restaurant operations

Thin margins leave no room for guessing where the money went. Daily transaction classification, vendor bill pay, and expense tracking give you a clear picture of food cost, beverage cost, and labor spend as they happen, not weeks later when the numbers are already stale.

Every invoice gets categorized correctly the first time. Bills get paid on schedule so vendor relationships stay solid, and receivables get tracked so nothing slips through. That level of daily discipline is what turns a stack of receipts into a report you can actually use to make decisions about staffing, menu pricing, or that new keg order.

The goal is simple: know your numbers in real time, not at month-end. Explore the full [bookkeeping services](/services/bookkeeping) built around this kind of daily-operation reality.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: restaurant-payroll-tip-reporting.jpg | alt: "Restaurant manager reviewing payroll and tip reports on a tablet" | query: "restaurant manager payroll tablet" -->
## Payroll and tip compliance made simple

Multi-shift schedules, tipped employees, and seasonal hires make restaurant payroll more complicated than most other small businesses face. Getting it wrong means penalties, back pay, or an uncomfortable conversation with the IRS. Getting it right frees you up to run the floor instead of chasing paperwork.

- Accurate processing for tipped, hourly, salaried, and seasonal staff
- Tip reporting handled correctly to meet IRS and state requirements
- Payroll tax filings submitted on time, every time
- Support for multi-location or multi-shift scheduling complexity
- Direct answers when a new hire or a wage question comes up mid-week

Payroll here isn't outsourced to a call center. Questions get answered by the same team that already knows your business. See how [payroll services](/what-we-do/payroll) fit into your bar or restaurant's weekly rhythm.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: restaurant-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA and restaurant owner discussing tax planning documents together" | query: "accountant restaurant owner tax planning" -->
## Tax planning and preparation for restaurant owners

A restaurant tax return should never feel like a surprise delivered in April. Sales tax rules for food and beverage sales in New York carry their own quirks, and missing a filing deadline or misclassifying a sale creates problems that compound over time.

Year-round planning means adjustments happen when they can still make a difference, not after the fiscal year closes. That includes reviewing entity structure, tracking deductible expenses specific to F&B operations, and flagging sales tax exposure before it becomes an issue with the state. Preparation happens on a secure digital platform, so documents move back and forth without a single trip to an office.

Restaurant owners in Port Chester and across Westchester County get a plan built around their calendar, their busy season, and their actual cash position, through [business tax services](/what-we-do/tax) designed for exactly this kind of complexity.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: restaurant-cost-margin-analysis.jpg | alt: "Advisor pointing to cost and margin charts with restaurant client" | query: "financial advisor restaurant charts" -->
## Advisory support to protect your margins

Cost of goods sold, labor cost percentage, and cash flow between busy and slow seasons determine whether a restaurant survives its second year. Watching those numbers only at tax time is too late to change anything.

Ongoing advisory support means someone is reviewing your margins alongside you throughout the year, not just reporting on them after the fact. That includes cash management to smooth out seasonal swings, guidance on labor cost ratios as staffing changes, and a second set of eyes before a lease renewal or menu overhaul. Stephen's background across construction, real estate, and hospitality means he's seen how cash pressure hits a small operation from multiple angles, not just one.

This is advisory work built for the reality of running a bar or restaurant, delivered through [advisory services](/services/advisory) and reinforced with [cash management](/what-we-do/cash-management) support when seasonal cash gets tight.

## Bookkeeping support built for busy business owners

Running a business in Port Chester means your attention is already split between customers, crews, staff, and suppliers. Bookkeeping shouldn't be one more thing competing for it. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA handles the daily work of transaction classification, expense tracking, bill payment, and invoicing so your books stay current without you touching a spreadsheet.

That's the idea behind our tagline: you run your business, we run your numbers. It's not a slogan we use loosely. When you hand off bookkeeping to our team, you get someone who actually looks at what's happening in your accounts each month, catches errors before they become problems, and flags anything that needs your attention. You stay informed without staying buried in the details.

For owners who've been doing their own books at night, or paying a part-time bookkeeper who disappears at tax time, this is a different kind of arrangement. One where the numbers are handled, and you know it.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: bookkeeping-services-checklist.jpg | alt: "Accountant organizing receipts and invoices for monthly bookkeeping" | query: "accountant organizing invoices receipts" -->
## What our monthly bookkeeping includes

Every client gets the same disciplined process, whether you're running a five-person contracting crew or a neighborhood bar. Each month, we reconcile your bank and credit card accounts, categorize every transaction, and keep your books ready before you ever need them to be.

- Bank and credit card reconciliation
- Transaction categorization and coding
- Accounts payable and bill payment
- Invoicing and accounts receivable tracking
- Monthly financial reporting and statements
- General ledger maintenance

Bookkeeping isn't sold on its own here. It's bundled with tax, payroll, and advisory support for one fixed monthly fee, so there's no surprise invoice for a phone call or a question about a transaction. Firms that bill by the hour tend to make clients think twice before reaching out. We'd rather you call.

## Real-time financial visibility through our secure platform

A lot of owners tell us the same thing before they become clients: they don't know where their money stands until someone tells them, and by then it's old news. Our secure online platform fixes that. You get real-time access to your financial data, reports, and documents whenever you need them, from wherever you are.

No more waiting for a quarterly meeting to find out if last month was actually profitable. No more digging through old email threads for a document you sent six months ago. Everything lives in one place, updated as we work, protected behind secure login credentials. If you want to check your cash position before signing a lease or hiring a fourth employee, you can, in the moment it matters.

## Bookkeeping tailored to construction, real estate, and bars and restaurants

General bookkeeping software can track expenses. It can't tell you which of your projects hemorrhaged the most in overtime last quarter, or whether your tip reporting would hold up under review. That takes bookkeeping built around how these industries actually make and lose money.

### Construction
icon: Hammer

Job costing is where most contractor books fall apart. We track labor, materials, and subcontractor costs by project so you know which jobs are actually profitable, not just whether the business overall is in the black. That visibility also keeps cash flow manageable between draw schedules and payment phases.

### Real Estate
icon: Building2

Whether you hold a handful of rental units or run a growing portfolio across multiple entities, your books need to reflect ownership structure accurately. We track income and expenses at the entity level and keep records organized for depreciation schedules and cost segregation opportunities your tax return can actually use.

### Bars and Restaurants
icon: Wallet

Thin margins mean every dollar has to be accounted for, from daily cash drawer counts to tip reporting to the vendor invoices that arrive every week. We reconcile sales, cash, and card deposits on the schedule your operation needs, so you always know what's landing in the bank versus what's just on paper.

## How we onboard your business

Switching bookkeepers, or handing off the job for the first time, feels risky. Our onboarding process is built so it doesn't feel that way.

### We start with a conversation
We ask how your business runs day to day: your existing systems, your software, your pain points, and what "on top of it" actually looks like for you.

### We review your current setup
If you're already using QuickBooks or another platform, we look at what's there, clean up what needs cleaning, and map out what stays and what changes.

### We build your books
We set up or migrate your accounts, establish your monthly reconciliation schedule, and connect you to our secure client platform.

### We keep talking
Onboarding isn't a one-time event. We check in as your business changes, because the way you operated at launch usually isn't how you'll operate at year three.

### Tax
URL: /services/tax

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Tax planning and preparation built around your life or business

Most tax prep shops show up in March and disappear in April. That works fine if your only tax question is "how much do I owe," but it falls apart the moment you're running a construction company with three jobs in progress, a rental portfolio, or a bar with tip reporting to track. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, LLC handles tax planning and preparation as a year-round relationship, not a once-a-year transaction.

Every client works from a secure online platform where you can see your financial data in real time, not just at filing season. Business and individual tax services are bundled into one fixed monthly fee, so there's no surprise invoice when a question comes up in July or a tax notice lands in October. You get a CPA who already knows your numbers, because we've been looking at them all year.

Whether you're filing a personal return, running a small business, or managing both, the goal is the same: fewer surprises, more planning, and a return that reflects decisions made months in advance, not scrambled together at the deadline.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: contractor-reviewing-tax-documents.jpg | alt: "Construction business owner reviewing tax documents with an accountant" | query: "contractor meeting accountant office" -->
## Business tax services for construction, real estate, and hospitality companies

Business tax preparation only works if the person preparing it understands how your business actually makes money. A general contractor's tax return should reflect job costing and profitability by project, not just a lump total of revenue and expense. A real estate investor's return needs to account for depreciation schedules that actually match the properties held. A bar or restaurant's return needs to reflect thin margins and cash flow that moves differently than a typical retail business.

Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, LLC prepares corporate and business tax returns with that context built in from the start, drawing on construction, real estate, and hospitality clients across Westchester County and the surrounding region. Planning happens throughout the year, not just before the filing deadline, so entity-level decisions, timing of major purchases, and depreciation strategy get addressed while there's still time to act on them.

This is business tax preparation and planning, delivered with the industry context to back it up. It's paired with [bookkeeping](/services/bookkeeping) and [payroll](/services/payroll) support, so the numbers feeding your return are accurate before they ever reach a tax form.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: individual-tax-planning-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing personal tax return with a client at a desk" | query: "accountant client reviewing paperwork" -->
## Personal income tax preparation with year-round planning

Tax software works if your financial life is simple. It gets shaky the moment you have side income, freelance work, rental property, or a small business woven into your personal return. And a one-time preparer who files your return and doesn't hear from you again for eleven months can't tell you to make an estimated payment in September or adjust withholding after a life change in June.

Personal income tax preparation with Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, LLC includes:

- Digital, secure return preparation with a CPA reviewing every line
- Year-round access to your preparer, not just a January-to-April window
- Proactive tax planning and projections so estimated payments and withholding stay on track
- Support for self-employed income, rental income, and small business owners filing personal returns
- A fixed monthly fee, so a mid-year question doesn't come with a surprise bill

Explore [personal income tax preparation](/what-we-do/personal-income-tax) or read our guide to [maximizing your tax refund](/resources/e-books/maximizing-your-tax-refund-a-strategic-guide-to-tax-planning) for a closer look at year-round planning.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: new-business-owner-consultation.jpg | alt: "New business owner discussing entity structure with a CPA" | query: "small business owner consultation meeting" -->
## Entity type analysis for new and growing businesses

Whether a new business should be an LLC, S-corp, or something else isn't a question with one right answer. It depends on projected income, how many owners are involved, whether real estate is held inside or outside the entity, and how the business plans to grow. Get it wrong early and it can mean years of paying more tax than necessary or restructuring later at a real cost.

Entity type analysis at Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, LLC walks new business owners through that decision with state and federal tax implications spelled out in plain terms, not jargon. It's especially relevant for construction companies weighing liability exposure, real estate investors deciding whether to hold property in separate entities, and restaurant or bar owners setting up a new location.

This service pairs naturally with [business foundation services](/what-we-do/business-foundation-services) for anyone launching a company from scratch, and with ongoing tax planning once the entity is in place. Learn more about [entity type analysis](/what-we-do/entity-type-analysis).

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Tax strategy for construction, real estate, and bar and restaurant owners

### Construction
icon: Hammer

Job costing complexity makes it hard to know which projects are actually profitable until the return is already filed. Tax planning for contractors ties into project-level tracking throughout the year, so income and expense timing, equipment purchases, and payroll costs are accounted for before year-end, not discovered after. Visit our [construction industry page](/industries/construction) for more.

### Real Estate
icon: Building2

Depreciation is one of the biggest tax levers a real estate investor has, and it's also one of the most commonly missed. Cost segregation opportunities and 1031 exchange timing both require planning well ahead of a transaction, not a scramble after closing. See how we support [real estate investors and owners](/industries/real-estate).

### Bars and Restaurants
icon: Receipt

Thin margins leave no room for guesswork on sales tax or tip reporting compliance. Bar and restaurant tax preparation has to reflect cash handling realities and multi-jurisdiction sales tax rules, tracked consistently so nothing gets flagged at filing time. Learn more on our [restaurant and bar industry page](/industries/restaurants).

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: outsourced-accounting-team.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing bookkeeping and payroll records on a laptop" | query: "accountant reviewing financial records office" -->
## What our outsourced accounting includes

Full charge outsourced accounting means every function that keeps your books accurate and your cash flow visible sits under one roof. Here's what's bundled into the monthly fee:

- Daily transaction classification and bookkeeping, so your books stay current instead of piling up for tax season
- Bank and credit card reconciliation, catching errors and discrepancies before they become problems
- Accounts payable management, including bill payment and vendor tracking
- Cash management, monitoring inflows and outflows so you always know where you stand
- Payroll coordination, keeping filings accurate and employees paid on time
- Tax integration, so your bookkeeping data flows directly into planning and preparation instead of getting reconstructed every spring

Each piece works together instead of living in separate spreadsheets or software subscriptions. That's the point of outsourcing the whole function instead of hiring around it, one task at a time.

## See your numbers in real time

Most accounting relationships run on a lag. You get a report weeks after the month closes, by which point the decision it should have informed is already made. That's not how we work.

Clients access a secure online platform built for real-time visibility into cash position, payables, and financial performance. No waiting for a monthly PDF. No guessing whether last week's numbers are still accurate.

If you're deciding whether to take on a new project, hire another server, or wait another quarter on a property purchase, you're making that call with current data instead of a stale snapshot. It's the same transparency you'd expect from an in-house controller, delivered without adding headcount.

## Helpful external links and resources

Some documents come from outside our office, and we'd rather point you to the source than make you dig for it. The IRS publishes current versions of every federal form at irs.gov/forms, including W-9, W-4, and 1099 variants. New York State's Department of Taxation and Finance (tax.ny.gov) maintains state withholding and sales tax forms, which matter most for our hospitality and construction clients filing across county lines. The U.S. Small Business Administration (sba.gov) is a solid starting point for licensing and entity formation questions before you talk to us about [entity type analysis](/what-we-do/entity-type-analysis) or [accounting system setup](/what-we-do/accounting-system-setup). Bookmark them if you like, but for anything specific to your return or your business, ask us first.

### Refund Tracker | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/refund-tracker

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Check your refund status with confidence

Waiting on a federal or New York State refund can feel like watching a pot that never boils. This page won't just point you to a government tracker and leave you guessing what the status codes mean. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA works with individuals and business owners across Port Chester, Westchester County, and beyond, translating "still processing" into plain language you can actually use.

If you filed with our team, you already have a direct line to ask questions. If you didn't, we're happy to look at your return, explain what the IRS or NY Department of Taxation and Finance status actually means, and flag anything that might need a follow-up. Refund tracking shouldn't require a decoder ring, and it shouldn't require an hour on hold either.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: refund-timeline-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing a client's tax return paperwork at a desk" | query: "accountant reviewing tax documents office" -->
## Why your refund timeline may differ

Refunds rarely arrive on a fixed schedule. A handful of common triggers explain most delays or changes to the amount you expected:

- Amended returns, which the IRS processes on a separate, slower timeline than original filings
- Credits claimed, like the Earned Income Tax Credit or Child Tax Credit, which require additional verification
- Entity type, since S-corps, partnerships, and sole proprietorships each flow through differently at tax time
- Withholding errors from payroll, which can shrink or inflate a refund without an obvious explanation
- Offsets for past-due taxes, child support, or other government debts
- Identity verification holds, especially for first-time filers or accounts with prior fraud flags

None of these mean something went wrong. They mean the return needs a closer look, and that's exactly the kind of detail Shawn Wilson, CPA and Denise Romano, CPA review with clients every filing season.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: individual-tax-refund-review.jpg | alt: "Client and accountant reviewing personal tax refund documents together" | query: "client accountant reviewing tax paperwork" -->
## Refund support for individuals and households

If you're an individual filer juggling a W-2, some freelance income, and a brokerage account, refund questions get complicated fast. Side income changes your estimated tax obligations. Investment gains and losses affect what you owe or get back. A missed deduction from last year can mean a smaller refund this year, and nobody wants to find that out after the fact.

We sit down with clients throughout Westchester County, Manhattan, Brooklyn, and as far as Asbury Park, NJ to walk through exactly what their refund status means and what to expect next filing season. Our [Personal Income Tax](/what-we-do/personal-income-tax) service includes year-round support, not just a rushed conversation in April, so you understand your withholding and estimated payments before they become a surprise.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Refund support for construction, real estate, and hospitality businesses

Business refunds work differently than personal ones, and the details shift again depending on your industry.

### Construction Companies
icon: Hammer

Retainage, job costing, and multi-phase contracts all affect how estimated payments line up with what a construction company eventually gets back. A refund tied to overpaid quarterly estimates often signals it's time to revisit cash flow projections between phases, not just file and forget. Our [construction](/industries/construction) clients get help matching job-level profitability to what shows up on the return.

### Real Estate Investors
icon: Building2

Depreciation schedules, cost segregation studies, and 1031 exchanges can all shift a refund up or down in ways that surprise even experienced investors. If a like-kind exchange wasn't structured correctly, an expected refund can turn into an unexpected bill. We review [real estate](/industries/real-estate) filings line by line before assuming a refund number is final.

### Bars and Restaurants
icon: Receipt

Thin margins, tip reporting, and sales tax complexity make refund timing especially unpredictable for bars and restaurants. Payroll tax filings tied to tipped employees can also affect what a business is owed. Our [restaurants and pub](/industries/restaurants) clients get a straight answer on what their refund reflects and what it doesn't.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: year-round-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Accountant and business owner reviewing financial data on a laptop" | query: "accountant business owner laptop meeting" -->
## Year-round tax planning means fewer refund surprises

A refund is really just a snapshot of last year's numbers. It tells you what already happened, not what's coming. That's why Stephen P. Pryor, CPA builds [tax planning](/what-we-do/tax) into a bundled monthly fee instead of treating it as a once-a-year scramble. Clients get access to a secure online platform showing real-time financial data, so estimated payments, withholding, and quarterly numbers stay visible all year, not just at filing time.

When you can see the numbers as they happen, a big refund or a surprise bill stops being a mystery. Construction, real estate, and hospitality clients in particular benefit from this, since project timing and seasonal cash flow make one-size-fits-all estimates unreliable.

### Bookkeeping | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /what-we-do/bookkeeping

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Local bookkeeping support that keeps your numbers current

If you run a business in Port Chester or anywhere else in Westchester County, you already know that clean books aren't optional. They're the foundation everything else sits on: your tax return, your payroll filings, your ability to answer the question "how are we actually doing?" without guessing. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA has built bookkeeping support around that reality, working with construction companies, real estate operators, and bars and restaurants across the region who need their numbers current, not caught up three months later.

We handle the daily grind of transaction coding, reconciliation, and reporting so you can answer the money questions that matter without digging through a shoebox of receipts. Tax season stops being a scramble because the work has already been done, month by month, all year.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: bookkeeping-daily-tasks.jpg | alt: "Bookkeeper organizing invoices and receipts at a desk" | query: "bookkeeper reviewing invoices desk" -->
## What our bookkeeping service covers

Bookkeeping means a lot of different things depending on who you ask. Here's what it actually includes when Stephen P. Pryor, CPA handles it for you:

- **Daily transaction classification**, every deposit, withdrawal, and charge gets coded correctly, so your financial reports reflect reality instead of a pile of miscategorized expenses.
- **Expense tracking**, we track what you're spending and where, so you can spot waste or opportunity before it becomes a bigger problem.
- **Bill payment**, vendor bills get paid on time, so you're not fielding late notices or damaging supplier relationships.
- **Invoicing**, invoices go out promptly and get tracked until they're paid, which matters for cash flow more than most owners realize.
- **Reconciliation**, bank and credit card accounts get matched against your books every month, catching errors, duplicate charges, or fraud early.

This isn't a once-a-year cleanup. It's ongoing work that keeps your books accurate all twelve months, which is exactly what makes tax time painless instead of stressful.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: real-time-financial-dashboard.jpg | alt: "Business owner viewing financial dashboard on a laptop" | query: "business owner laptop financial dashboard" -->
## Real-time financial data through a secure online platform

A lot of small business owners in Westchester County are still working with a bookkeeper who mails a report once a quarter, if you're lucky. That's not how we operate. Clients access their financial data through a secure online platform, any time, from a laptop or phone, without waiting on a callback or an email.

That means you can check your cash position before making a hiring decision, pull up last month's numbers before a lender meeting, or see exactly where a project stands financially without asking us to run a report first. The platform keeps your data current and protected, which matters as much as the convenience. You get visibility into your business on your schedule, not ours.

## Business tax preparation for construction, real estate, and hospitality

Construction contractors, real estate investors, and bar owners across Westchester County don't file the same return as a retail shop, and treating them the same way is where a lot of tax prep goes wrong. For [construction](/industries/construction) businesses, that means tracking job costs by project so profitability shows up correctly on the return, not just in a spreadsheet nobody reconciles. For [real estate](/industries/real-estate) clients, it means reviewing depreciation schedules and cost segregation opportunities before year-end, and structuring 1031 exchanges so a sale doesn't trigger a tax bill nobody planned for.

[Bars and restaurants](/industries/restaurants) bring their own set of problems: thin margins, tip reporting, and sales tax rules that vary by what's sold and where. We've built our tax preparation process around these specifics, not a generic template. Firm founder Stephen Pryor built the practice on construction, real estate, and hospitality work, with a particular focus on bars and pubs, so the return reflects how the business runs, not how a generic tax program assumes it runs.

## Personal income tax preparation and planning

Filing a return once a year and hoping for the best isn't planning. It's guessing.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: tax-projection-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant walking a client through a quarterly tax projection report" | query: "advisor client reviewing financial report" -->
## Year-round tax planning and projections, not just filing

Most tax prep shops see you once a year, hand you a bill or a refund, and see you again next April. That model works fine until a mid-year decision, a new hire, a property purchase, an entity change, has real tax consequences nobody flagged in time. Our planning process runs alongside your business all year:

- [Entity type analysis](/what-we-do/entity-type-analysis) to confirm your structure (S-corp, LLC, partnership) fits your current income, not the one that made sense five years ago
- [Retirement plan analysis](/what-we-do/retirement-plan-analysis) to find a plan that fits your budget and lowers taxable income
- Quarterly estimated tax projections so there's no surprise balance due in April
- Mid-year check-ins before major decisions, a sale, a purchase, a new hire, not after

That matters most for bar and restaurant clients managing tip reporting and construction clients tracking labor costs across multiple job sites.

LLC, S-corp, partnership, sole proprietorship: each one changes how you're taxed, what you owe in self-employment tax, and how much paperwork you'll file every year. Pick wrong and restructuring later means legal fees, new filings, and sometimes a tax bill you didn't see coming.

### 5 Tips to Build a Healthy Money Mindset and Grow Your Finances | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/5-tips-to-build-a-healthy-money-mindset-and-grow-your-finances

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Why your relationship with money shapes your financial future

Most people think financial success comes down to income. It rarely does. We've sat across the table from business owners pulling six figures who still feel like money slips through their fingers, and we've watched careful savers on modest paychecks build real security. The difference is mindset: how you think about money, track it, and plan around it.

As a CPA firm in Port Chester, NY, we spend less time on tax forms than you'd expect and more time listening. Clients come to us stressed about cash flow, confused about deductions, or just tired of guessing. These five habits are the ones we see change outcomes, whether you run a construction company, own a rental property, or manage a neighborhood bar. None require an accounting degree. They just require a shift in how you approach the numbers.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: money-tracking-clarity.jpg | alt: "Small business owner reviewing spending records on a laptop" | query: "person reviewing finances laptop" -->
## Start with clarity on where your money goes

You can't fix a problem you can't see. That's the first thing we tell new clients, whether they're a household juggling two incomes or a contractor managing five job sites. Most financial stress isn't about not having enough money. It's about not knowing where it went.

Tracking doesn't need to be complicated. Start with your bank and credit card statements from the last three months and sort spending into a handful of categories. Business owners in construction and real estate often discover the leak isn't a big purchase, it's a pile of small recurring charges nobody reviewed.

This is exactly what our [bookkeeping](/what-we-do/bookkeeping) service handles day to day: transaction classification, expense tracking, and invoicing, delivered through a secure online platform so you can check your numbers anytime instead of waiting for a year-end surprise.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: tax-planning-calendar.jpg | alt: "Calendar and financial documents laid out for year-round tax planning" | query: "tax planning calendar documents" -->
## Plan ahead instead of reacting at tax time

Reactive tax filing, scrambling in March with a shoebox of receipts, is one of the most common sources of financial stress we see. It's also one of the easiest to fix. The shift is simple: stop treating taxes as a once-a-year event and start treating them as an ongoing conversation.

Quarterly check-ins let you adjust withholding, time large purchases, or restructure income before December 31, not after. For real estate owners, that might mean timing a 1031 exchange correctly. For a restaurant owner, it might mean planning around seasonal cash flow before payroll tax deadlines hit.

Our [tax](/what-we-do/tax) team builds personalized, year-round projections instead of a single annual appointment, so decisions get made with real numbers instead of guesses. Individuals with side income or investment gains benefit the same way through our [personal income tax](/what-we-do/personal-income-tax) support.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: organized-accounting-systems.jpg | alt: "Organized office desk with accounting binders and a laptop showing financial reports" | query: "organized office accounting workspace" -->
## Build systems that reduce daily financial stress

A healthy money mindset isn't just a feeling, it's supported by systems that do the worrying for you. Business owners in construction, real estate, and hospitality carry extra weight here: payroll deadlines, job costing, tip reporting, and cash flow that swings with the seasons.

The fix is building infrastructure once so it runs quietly in the background:

- Set up an accounting system matched to your industry, not a generic template
- Automate payroll so filings and deposits happen on time, every time
- Track cash flow weekly instead of discovering shortfalls at month's end
- Separate business and personal accounts from day one
- Review job costing or per-project profitability on a fixed schedule

This is where our [accounting system setup](/what-we-do/accounting-system-setup), [payroll](/what-we-do/payroll), and [cash management](/what-we-do/cash-management) services fit together, bundled for a fixed monthly fee so there's no guesswork about cost as your business grows.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: financial-goal-review-meeting.jpg | alt: "Advisor and client reviewing financial goals during a check-in meeting" | query: "advisor client meeting reviewing goals" -->
## Set realistic goals and revisit them regularly

A goal you set once in January and never look at again isn't a plan, it's a wish. Money mindset improves when goals get revisited on a schedule: paying down a specific debt, hitting a savings target, or growing revenue by a defined percentage this year.

We build this into the relationship rather than treating it as a once-a-year event. A construction business tracking profitability per project needs a different check-in rhythm than a household saving for a home purchase, but both benefit from someone asking, "Is this still working?" every quarter instead of every April.

That ongoing rhythm is the difference between advice and advisory. It's also why clients stay with us for years rather than filing once and disappearing.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: cpa-consultation-westchester.jpg | alt: "CPA meeting with a small business owner in Westchester County office" | query: "CPA meeting small business owner" -->
## Know when to bring in a trusted financial partner

At some point, a spreadsheet and good intentions aren't enough. That's usually when a business adds employees, buys a second property, or a household's tax situation gets more complicated than a standard return. Knowing when to ask for help is itself part of a healthy money mindset.

Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, and Shawn Wilson, CPA, work with construction, real estate, and hospitality clients across Westchester County, including Port Chester, along with Manhattan, Brooklyn, and clients as far as Asbury Park, NJ. Denise Romano, CPA, and the firm's involvement with the Greenwich First Advisory Boards keep the team plugged into the local business community, not just the tax code.

What clients notice most isn't a specific software or form. It's that we take the time during onboarding to actually learn how your business runs before we touch a single number.

### Report Suggests 40% of Workers Have Used AI to Make Fake Expense Receipts | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/report-suggests-40-of-workers-have-used-ai-to-make-fake-expense-receipts

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## AI made receipt fraud easier to fake and harder to spot

A recent report found that 40% of workers admit to using AI tools to create fake expense receipts. Five years ago, that number would have seemed impossible. Today, generative AI can produce a convincing restaurant receipt, gas station printout, or vendor invoice in seconds, complete with realistic totals, tax lines, and logos.

For business owners who approve reimbursements with a quick glance, that visual check is losing its power. A receipt that looks legitimate no longer means it is. This isn't a large-corporation problem. Any business that reimburses employees, contractors, or vendors for out-of-pocket costs is exposed, and most small and mid-sized companies still rely on manual review as their only safeguard.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: construction-manager-reviewing-receipts.jpg | alt: "Construction site manager reviewing paper receipts and invoices at a desk" | query: "construction manager reviewing receipts paperwork" -->
## Why small and mid-sized businesses in Westchester County are especially exposed

Construction, real estate, and hospitality businesses process a high volume of reimbursable expenses: job materials, subcontractor payments, per diems, vendor deposits. That volume, paired with the fast pace of running a jobsite or a bar, often means expense review happens quickly and without much structure.

A construction company juggling several active projects may not have time to verify every material receipt against a purchase order. A bar or restaurant owner handling cash tips, vendor deliveries, and staff reimbursements at the same time has even less bandwidth. These are exactly the conditions where a fabricated receipt slips through: high transaction counts, thin administrative staffing, and trust built on years of working with the same vendors and crew.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: hands-sorting-expense-receipts.jpg | alt: "Close-up of hands sorting through a stack of paper expense receipts" | query: "hands sorting expense receipts paperwork" -->
## Warning signs your expense reporting process may be vulnerable

Most fake receipts don't announce themselves. They show up as small inconsistencies that get missed when review happens fast. A few patterns worth a second look:

- Receipts from the same vendor with inconsistent formatting, fonts, or logo placement
- Suspiciously round dollar totals with no itemization
- Missing tax lines, order numbers, or other details a real receipt would include
- Expenses submitted weeks after the purchase date with no explanation
- The same employee submitting reimbursements just under an approval threshold, repeatedly

None of these confirm fraud on their own. But a pattern of them is a signal that your current review process, whatever it is, needs a closer set of eyes on it.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: bookkeeper-reviewing-financial-records.jpg | alt: "Bookkeeper reviewing financial records and receipts on a laptop screen" | query: "bookkeeper reviewing financial documents laptop" -->
## How a fixed-fee bookkeeping and advisory partner reduces this risk

AI-generated receipts are built to pass a visual check. They're not built to survive a cross-reference against your bank activity, vendor history, and job costs, which is exactly the kind of review that comes standard with [bookkeeping](/what-we-do/bookkeeping) done by someone who knows your business, not just your paperwork.

Our bundled bookkeeping and [outsourced accounting](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting) services combine daily transaction classification with a secure online platform that gives you real-time visibility into what's being spent and where. When something doesn't match, an unfamiliar vendor, a total that doesn't line up with a job's actual materials cost, a pattern of near-threshold submissions, it gets flagged during normal reconciliation, not discovered months later during tax prep. That's the difference between catching a problem and cleaning one up.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: colleagues-discussing-expense-report.jpg | alt: "Two colleagues discussing an expense report together at a desk" | query: "colleagues discussing expense report desk" -->
## Simple steps to strengthen your expense controls today

You don't need a full systems overhaul to close the gaps AI-generated receipts exploit. A few practical changes go a long way:

- Require a second approver for reimbursements over a set dollar amount
- Match receipts against corresponding bank or credit card charges before reimbursing
- Ask for itemized receipts rather than accepting a total-only printout
- Run a periodic spot-check on a sample of past reimbursements, not just new ones
- Set up your accounting system so expense categories and vendors are consistent, making outliers easier to spot

Each of these takes minutes to put in place and none of them requires new software or a new hire, just a bit more structure around a process that may currently run on trust alone.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: cpa-consultation-handshake.jpg | alt: "Business owner and CPA shaking hands after a consultation meeting" | query: "business owner accountant handshake meeting" -->
## Talk with a Westchester County CPA about protecting your business

If you're not sure how exposed your current expense process is, that's a normal place to start from, not a problem you should already have solved. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA works with construction, real estate, and hospitality businesses across Westchester County and beyond to build bookkeeping oversight that catches issues like this before they become expensive ones.

[Schedule a consultation](/contact) and we'll walk through your current process, point out where the gaps are, and talk about what a fixed-fee bookkeeping partnership would look like for your business.

### 4 Steps to Get Ahead of Higher Taxes | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/4-steps-to-get-ahead-of-higher-taxes

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Why proactive tax planning matters more than ever

If your tax bill keeps surprising you every April, you're not alone. Federal brackets shift, New York State keeps its own rules, and Westchester County property and local taxes add another layer on top. Waiting until tax season to think about any of it means you've already missed most of your options.

Proactive tax planning flips that script. Instead of reacting to a number your accountant hands you in March, you're making decisions in June, September, and December that shape what that number looks like. For business owners in Port Chester running construction crews, managing rental properties, or pouring drinks behind a bar, that difference can mean thousands of dollars kept in the business instead of sent to the IRS.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: contractor-reviewing-tax-documents.jpg | alt: "Construction business owner reviewing financial paperwork with a calculator" | query: "contractor reviewing paperwork office" -->
## Step one: review your entity structure and income timing

How your business is legally structured, sole proprietorship, LLC, S-corp, or partnership, determines how much you pay in self-employment tax, what deductions are available, and how income flows to your personal return. A lot of construction and real estate owners set up their entity years ago and never revisit it, even as revenue grows or ownership changes.

Income timing matters just as much. Deferring a large invoice into January, accelerating a deductible equipment purchase into December, or timing a property sale around other income can shift your effective tax rate meaningfully. These aren't one-size-fits-all moves. What works for a two-person plumbing business looks different from what works for a real estate investor holding three rental properties. Our [entity type analysis](/what-we-do/entity-type-analysis) work walks through the state and federal tradeoffs before you commit to a structure, not after.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: restaurant-owner-financial-review.jpg | alt: "Restaurant owner reviewing sales and tax records at a bar counter" | query: "restaurant owner reviewing financial records" -->
## Step two: maximize deductions and industry-specific credits

This is where most of the money gets left on the table. General deduction advice misses the details that actually matter in your industry.

- **Construction:** Job costing that separates labor, materials, and overhead per project, plus depreciation strategy on trucks, tools, and heavy equipment
- **Real estate:** Cost segregation studies that accelerate depreciation, and 1031 exchange timing that defers capital gains without tripping IRS rules
- **Bars and restaurants:** Tip credit calculations, proper cash handling documentation, and sales tax nuances that vary depending on what's served and how

A generalist tax preparer might catch the basics. A CPA who's worked inside these industries catches the rest. If you've never had someone walk through your books looking specifically for construction, real estate, or hospitality deductions, there's a good chance you're overpaying.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: retirement-planning-discussion.jpg | alt: "Small business owner discussing retirement plan options with an advisor" | query: "business owner retirement planning meeting" -->
## Step three: plan for retirement and long-term tax efficiency

Retirement contributions are one of the few tax moves that reduce your bill today while building something for later. The problem is choosing the right plan. A Solo 401(k), SEP IRA, or SIMPLE IRA each come with different contribution limits, deadlines, and administrative requirements, and the right fit depends on your income, whether you have employees, and how much cash flow flexibility you need.

For a construction business owner with fluctuating annual income, or a real estate investor managing multiple entities, the wrong plan can mean lower contribution limits than necessary or paperwork headaches that outweigh the tax benefit. Our [retirement plan analysis](/what-we-do/retirement-plan-analysis) service matches the plan to your actual numbers, not a generic recommendation.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: cpa-client-year-round-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA and small business client reviewing financial data on a laptop together" | query: "accountant client meeting laptop" -->
## Step four: build a year-round relationship with your CPA

Tax planning doesn't happen in one meeting. It happens through decisions made all twelve months of the year, and that requires an accountant who's actually looking at your numbers between filings, not just in the weeks before a deadline.

That's the model we built the firm around. Clients get [bookkeeping](/what-we-do/bookkeeping), [payroll](/what-we-do/payroll), and [tax](/what-we-do/tax) support bundled for one fixed monthly fee, with a secure online platform showing real-time financial data instead of last quarter's numbers. When something changes in your business, a new hire, a property purchase, a slow season, we're already looking at the same data you are. Stephen Pryor, CPA, Shawn Wilson, CPA, and Denise Romano, CPA lead that ongoing work for clients across Port Chester and the rest of Westchester County.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: business-owner-handshake-cpa.jpg | alt: "Business owner shaking hands with a CPA advisor in an office" | query: "handshake business meeting office" -->
## Get a personalized tax strategy built around your business

Every construction company, restaurant, and real estate portfolio carries a different tax story. A generic checklist won't catch what's specific to yours, but a CPA who's spent time in your industry will. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA works with business owners and individuals across Port Chester and Westchester County to build tax strategies around entity structure, industry-specific deductions, retirement planning, and cash flow, all supported year-round instead of once a year.

If you're ready to stop guessing at your tax bill, [schedule a consultation](/contact) and let's look at your numbers together.

### Personal Income Tax | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /what-we-do/personal-income-tax

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Personal tax support that goes beyond filing a return

Filing your personal tax return shouldn't feel like a scramble every April. At Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, individual tax work is a year-round relationship, not a once-a-year transaction. We work with people across Port Chester and Westchester County who want a straightforward answer when a tax question comes up in June, not just a rushed conversation in March.

Stephen Pryor, Shawn Wilson, and Denise Romano, all CPAs, review your return with the same attention whether you're a salaried employee, a freelancer with side income, or someone drawing retirement income for the first time. You get secure, real-time access to your documents and return status through our online platform, so you're never left guessing where things stand.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: personal-tax-documents-review.jpg | alt: "CPA reviewing personal tax documents with a client at a desk" | query: "accountant reviewing tax documents client" -->
## What our personal income tax service includes

Every personal tax engagement starts with a real conversation about your finances, not a questionnaire. From there, we build a return and a plan around what's actually happening in your life.

- **Form 1040 preparation**: Complete personal tax returns prepared with attention to every deduction and credit you qualify for, delivered digitally and explained in plain language.
- **Self-employed and side income tax handling**: If you freelance, drive for a rideshare service, or run a side business alongside your job, we track the deductions and quarterly estimates that keep you from a surprise bill.
- **Investment income tax**: Capital gains, dividends, and interest income get reported correctly, with an eye toward tax-efficient timing when you're deciding when to sell.
- **Retirement income tax planning**: Social Security, pension distributions, and IRA withdrawals each carry different tax rules. We help you sequence withdrawals to keep more of what you've saved.
- **Year-round tax planning and projections**: Instead of waiting until January, we run projections throughout the year so you know what you owe well before the deadline arrives.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: individual-tax-planning-conversation.jpg | alt: "Client and accountant discussing personal tax planning documents" | query: "client accountant discussion office" -->
## Common tax challenges we help individuals solve

Most people who come to us aren't confused about taxes in general. They're confused about their taxes: the specific mix of a W-2 job, a rental property, some stock sales, and maybe a small side business that all need to fit together on one return.

If you're between 35 and 60, chances are your financial picture has gotten more complicated over the past decade. A promotion came with stock options. A parent needed help with a down payment. Side income from consulting or a side business showed up on a 1099 you weren't expecting.

The most common problem we see isn't a mistake on last year's return. It's a missed opportunity from the year before that, a deduction nobody flagged because nobody was looking until tax season was already underway. Year-round planning catches those before the filing deadline, not after.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: real-estate-investor-tax-planning.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing property and tax records with an accountant" | query: "business owner reviewing financial records" -->
## Tax planning for business owners and real estate investors

If you own a construction company, a restaurant, or rental property, your personal return and your business return are connected in ways a generic tax preparer might miss. Depreciation decisions on a rental property affect your personal tax liability for years. A pass-through entity structure changes what shows up on your Schedule E or Schedule C.

Stephen Pryor, Shawn Wilson, and Denise Romano work with construction, real estate, and hospitality business owners regularly, which means personal tax planning happens alongside the business numbers, not separately from them. We look at cost segregation opportunities on investment properties, entity structure implications for owner-operators, and how business income timing affects your personal bracket, so decisions made in your business don't create surprises on your 1040.

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: vertical -->

A short conversation about a job change, a new rental property, or side income tells us what needs extra attention before we start preparing anything.
