### Entity Type Analysis | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /what-we-do/entity-type-analysis

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Choosing the right entity shapes your taxes for years to come

The entity you pick when you start a business, or the one you inherited when you took over from a parent or partner, quietly controls a lot: what you owe the IRS every April, how exposed your personal assets are if something goes wrong, and how easily you can bring in investors or sell down the road. Most owners make this call once, early on, often based on a quick answer from a lawyer or a form they found online. That decision doesn't have to be permanent, and it doesn't have to be a guess.

Whether you're structuring a brand-new company or wondering if the LLC you set up eight years ago still fits, entity type analysis gives you a clear answer grounded in your numbers, not a generic template. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, and Shawn Wilson, CPA, walk through the tradeoffs with you in plain language, so you understand the why behind the recommendation.

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: vertical -->
## How we evaluate your options

Entity selection isn't a single calculation. It's a handful of questions, answered honestly, that point toward sole proprietorship, partnership, S-corp, C-corp, or LLC.

### Understand your income goals

We start with where the business is headed financially: current revenue, projected growth, and how much of that income you plan to reinvest versus draw out personally.

### Assess your liability exposure

Some structures shield personal assets better than others. We look at your industry risk, contracts, and whether liability protection should outweigh simpler tax treatment.

### Map your growth plans

Bringing on partners, raising capital, or eventually selling the business all favor different entity types. We factor in where you want to be in five or ten years, not just today.

### Weigh state and federal tax implications

New York, Connecticut, New Jersey, and Florida each treat entity types differently for state tax purposes. We run the numbers across federal and state obligations before recommending a structure.

### Recommend a structure and explain the reasoning

You get a clear recommendation, in plain terms, along with the math behind it, so you can make the final call with confidence instead of guesswork.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Support for construction, real estate, and hospitality businesses

Entity structure decisions rarely play out the same way twice. A contractor juggling three active job sites has different liability concerns than a bar owner handling cash receipts every night. We built our approach around the industries we know best.

### Construction

icon: Hammer

Job costing and bonding requirements often push contractors toward multi-entity structures, separating equipment ownership from operations to protect assets project by project. We help you weigh whether that separation makes sense given your project volume and crew size.

### Real Estate

icon: Home

Holding companies can separate liability from individual properties and make cost segregation and 1031 exchange planning cleaner down the line. We look at your portfolio size and acquisition plans before recommending how to structure each asset.

### Bars and Restaurants

icon: Receipt

Ownership structures for bars and pubs need to account for thin margins, tip reporting, and sales tax exposure across one location or several. We've worked through these questions with hospitality owners in Westchester County and beyond, and know where the tax traps usually sit.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: business-owner-reviewing-structure.jpg | alt: "Business owner and CPA reviewing entity structure documents at a desk" | query: "small business owner meeting accountant" -->
## Revisiting your structure as your business grows

A lot of business owners set up their LLC or S-corp years ago, when revenue was smaller and the future looked different, and never looked at it again. That's normal. It's also often costly. As income climbs, an S-corp election can trim self-employment tax that a sole proprietorship or straight LLC leaves on the table. As liability exposure grows, a single-entity structure that made sense at $200,000 in revenue might leave too much exposed at $2 million.

We treat entity review as something to revisit periodically, not a one-time box to check. If your revenue, ownership, or risk profile has shifted since your last filing, it's worth twenty minutes to find out whether your current structure still fits or whether a change could mean real savings and better protection.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: online-platform-financial-data.jpg | alt: "Laptop screen showing secure financial dashboard with business data" | query: "laptop financial dashboard business owner" -->
## Entity analysis as part of your year-round partnership

Entity type analysis isn't a stand-alone project we hand off and forget. It's folded into the same fixed monthly fee that covers your bookkeeping, tax, and payroll work, so revisiting your structure doesn't mean a new invoice or a new conversation from scratch.

- One fixed monthly fee covers entity analysis alongside bookkeeping, tax, and payroll, no surprise bills for a structure review
- A secure online platform gives you real-time visibility into the numbers behind any recommendation, so you're never guessing at the math
- Personalized, year-round support means questions about your structure get answered when they come up, not just at tax time
- We already know your books and your industry, from construction job costing to bar and restaurant cash flow, so recommendations are grounded in your actual numbers

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: consultation-handshake-office.jpg | alt: "Business owner and CPA shaking hands after a consultation" | query: "business owner accountant consultation handshake" -->
## Talk with us about your business structure

If you're launching a new construction company, real estate venture, or bar, or you've had the same entity in place for years and haven't checked whether it still fits, we'll listen to where your business stands and walk through the options with you. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, Shawn Wilson, CPA, and Denise Romano, CPA, bring the same close-listening approach to every client, new or long-standing.

[Schedule a consultation](/contact) and let's talk through what structure actually fits your business today.

### Accounting System Setup | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## A stronger financial foundation starts with the right system

Most accounting headaches trace back to one thing: a system that was never set up right in the first place. Maybe you're running QuickBooks with a chart of accounts that made sense three years ago but not anymore. Maybe your bank feeds aren't connected, so someone still enters transactions by hand every week. Maybe there's no real system at all yet, just a shoebox of receipts and good intentions.

Stephen P. Pryor, CPA builds accounting systems for Port Chester business owners who need more than software installed and left alone. We look at how your business runs day to day, then set up a system that matches it, not a generic template. That's the foundation everything else depends on: clean bookkeeping, accurate payroll, and tax planning that's based on real numbers instead of guesswork.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: accounting-system-configuration.jpg | alt: "Accountant configuring bookkeeping software on a laptop for a small business" | query: "accountant setting up bookkeeping software" -->
## What our accounting system setup includes

Setting up a system is more than picking software off a shelf. Before we touch a single setting, we learn how your business operates: how invoices go out, how bills get paid, how you track jobs, properties, or nightly sales. Then we build around it.

- Selecting and configuring the right platform for your business, whether that's QuickBooks Online, QuickBooks Desktop, or another platform suited to your industry
- Building a chart of accounts that reflects how you make decisions, not a generic template pulled from a manual
- Connecting bank and credit card feeds so transactions flow in automatically instead of getting entered by hand
- Integrating payroll and invoicing so everything lands in one place instead of three different systems
- Establishing workflows and approval steps that match how your team [already works](/what-we-do/bookkeeping), rather than forcing you to adapt to the software

We cover this during onboarding, when we're learning your internal systems anyway, so the setup work doesn't feel like a separate project bolted onto everything else.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Set up to match how your industry works

### Construction
icon: Hammer

Job costing is where most contractors lose track of profitability. We set up systems that tie labor, materials, and subcontractor costs back to individual jobs, so you know which projects make money and which ones quietly don't, before the job is finished instead of after.

### Real estate
icon: Building2

Property and entity tracking gets complicated fast when you're managing multiple LLCs, mixed-use properties, or a growing portfolio. We build charts of accounts and reporting structures that keep each property and entity separate and clean, so depreciation, cash flow, and 1031 planning stay accurate instead of tangled together.

### Bars and restaurants
icon: Receipt

Sales tax, tip reporting, and thin margins demand a system that connects your point-of-sale to your books automatically. We set up POS integrations that capture daily sales, tips, and sales tax correctly from day one, so nothing gets reconciled by hand at month-end, and you can see where the money actually goes.

This is why we cover [construction](/industries/construction), [real estate](/industries/real-estate), and [restaurants and bars](/industries/restaurants) as core industries, not side specialties. The setup work looks different for each one, and it should.

Once your system is built, you shouldn't have to wait for a monthly report to know where you stand. Every accounting system we set up connects to a secure online platform where you can see your numbers in real time: cash balances, outstanding invoices, payroll costs, whenever you need them.

That visibility is the difference between reacting to last quarter's numbers and making decisions with this week's. It's also what makes our bundled monthly service work: one fixed fee covers bookkeeping, payroll, and advisory support, all built on the same system and platform, so nothing falls through the cracks between services.

### Retirement Plan Analysis | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /what-we-do/retirement-plan-analysis

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: retirement-plan-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA and small business owner reviewing retirement plan documents at a desk" | query: "advisor client reviewing financial documents" -->
## Retirement planning built around your business, not a generic template

Running a construction crew, managing rental units, or keeping a bar open on a busy Friday night doesn't leave much room to think about retirement. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA works with business owners across Port Chester and Westchester County who need a plan shaped around how their money actually moves, not a product pulled off a shelf. Before recommending anything, we look at your entity structure, your cash flow patterns, and where you want to be in ten years.

A SEP IRA that fits a real estate investor with steady rental income might create the wrong tax outcome for a restaurant owner managing seasonal swings. That gap is exactly why retirement plan analysis works better as advice from a CPA who already knows your books than as a pitch from someone meeting you for the first time. [Learn more about Stephen's background](/who-we-are/stephen-pryor).

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: retirement-plan-options.jpg | alt: "Business owner comparing retirement account paperwork with an accountant" | query: "small business owner financial planning meeting" -->
## Finding the right plan for your budget and goals

Retirement plan analysis starts with numbers, not a sales pitch. We review your revenue, payroll structure, and profit margins to figure out which qualified plan fits your budget this year and where you're headed longer term. A solo owner with no employees has different options than a contractor running crews of fifteen, and the right answer changes depending on which one you are.

Here's what we typically evaluate:

- SEP IRA for simplicity and flexible annual contributions
- Solo 401(k) for owner-only businesses wanting higher contribution limits
- SIMPLE IRA for small teams needing an affordable employer match
- Defined benefit plans for owners looking to shelter larger amounts of income
- Traditional and Roth IRA coordination alongside business retirement accounts

We explain the tradeoffs in plain language, then help you set up and fund the plan that actually matches your goals.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: construction-real-estate-retirement.jpg | alt: "Construction business owner and real estate professional reviewing financial plans" | query: "construction contractor reviewing paperwork office" -->
## Retirement strategy for construction and real estate business owners

Construction income rarely arrives on a predictable schedule. A strong month during framing season can be followed by a slow stretch waiting on a permit or a client payment. Retirement contributions need to flex with that reality, which is why a plan with variable annual funding, like a SEP IRA, often fits better than a rigid contribution schedule.

Real estate professionals face a different puzzle. Rental income and property sales can create passive income alongside self-employment earnings from brokerage or property management work, and getting the entity structure right affects both your tax bill and how much you can shelter for retirement. Stephen has worked with [construction firms](/industries/construction) and [real estate businesses](/industries/real-estate) across Westchester County long enough to know where those situations overlap and where they don't.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: bar-restaurant-owner-planning.jpg | alt: "Bar owner reviewing financial paperwork behind the counter after hours" | query: "restaurant owner reviewing finances after hours" -->
## Retirement planning for bar and restaurant owners

Bar and restaurant margins run thin even in a good year, and cash flow can swing hard between a quiet Tuesday and a packed Saturday. Owners often assume retirement planning has to wait until the business is more stable. It doesn't have to.

Plans like a SEP IRA let you contribute more in strong months and less when things tighten, without locking you into a fixed schedule you can't meet. We've built retirement strategies for [bar and pub owners](/industries/restaurants) around Port Chester who needed something flexible enough to bend with a seasonal calendar and unpredictable tip income, while still lowering their tax bill.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How retirement plan analysis fits into your overall tax strategy

Retirement plan analysis isn't a form you file once and forget. Contribution decisions affect your tax return every year, and they work best when coordinated with the rest of your planning instead of handled in isolation. That's why this service connects directly to the [year-round tax planning](/what-we-do/tax) support delivered through our secure online platform.

As your income changes, your contribution strategy might need to change with it. We review that alongside your quarterly estimates and year-end projections, so retirement planning isn't something that only comes up once a year around tax season.

### Cash Management | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /what-we-do/cash-management

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Cash flow is the lifeline of your business

A profitable month on paper doesn't always mean money in the bank when payroll's due. Businesses close every year not because they lacked profit, but because cash ran out at the wrong moment: a client paid late, a big invoice came due before the next check cleared, a slow season stretched longer than the reserve could cover.

Stephen Pryor works through these gaps with clients before they turn into emergencies. Real cash management means watching what comes in and what goes out on a regular schedule, not scrambling to explain a shortfall after it happens. Whether you're a [construction](/industries/construction) firm waiting on progress payments, a restaurant riding weekend swings, or a real estate investor timing a refinance, the goal is the same: know your position today and plan three months out with confidence.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: cpa-reviewing-cash-flow-report.jpg | alt: "CPA and business owner reviewing a cash flow report on a laptop" | query: "accountant reviewing financial report client" -->
## What our cash management service includes

Cash management isn't a once-a-year report. It's a habit built into how your [bookkeeping](/what-we-do/bookkeeping) gets run every week. Here's what's part of the service:

- Ongoing tracking of cash inflows and outflows across every account you operate
- Rolling forecasts that flag a shortfall weeks before it hits, not after
- Real-time access to your numbers through our secure online platform, so you're never waiting on an email to know where you stand
- Scheduled check-ins to walk through trends, seasonal dips, and upcoming obligations
- Direct coordination with your bookkeeping and tax data, so cash decisions are based on accurate numbers instead of guesswork

The point is simple: fewer surprises, more lead time. When you can see a gap coming three or four weeks out, you have options, drawing on a line of credit, adjusting a payment schedule, holding off on a purchase. When you find out the week it happens, you don't.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: contractor-reviewing-project-costs.jpg | alt: "Construction contractor reviewing project cost documents on a job site" | query: "construction contractor reviewing paperwork jobsite" -->
## Cash management built for construction companies

Construction cash flow doesn't move in a straight line. Money goes out for materials and subcontractors well before a progress payment comes in, and retainage can sit held back for months after a job wraps. A contractor with three jobs running at different phases can look profitable on the year-end statement and still come up short in March.

We track cash by project and in aggregate, so you can see which jobs are funding the business right now and which ones are waiting on retainage or a final draw. That visibility helps with timing equipment purchases, payroll during slow stretches, and deciding when to bid on the next job instead of waiting to see what's left in the account.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: real-estate-investor-reviewing-portfolio.jpg | alt: "Real estate investor reviewing rental property financials at a desk" | query: "real estate investor reviewing property documents" -->
## Cash management for real estate investors and businesses

Rental income arrives on a schedule; expenses don't always cooperate with it. A roof repair, a vacancy, or a refinance that closes later than planned can pull cash reserves down fast if there's no plan sitting behind the rent roll.

We help landlords and [real estate](/industries/real-estate) operators build reserve targets property by property, so a single capital expenditure doesn't derail the portfolio. When you're planning an acquisition or coordinating the timing of a refinance, we look at how it affects cash on hand across everything you own, not just the one deal in front of you. That coordination is what keeps a growing portfolio from outrunning its own cash position.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: bar-owner-reviewing-daily-sales.jpg | alt: "Bar owner reviewing daily sales and cash reports at the counter" | query: "restaurant owner reviewing sales reports" -->
## Cash management for bars and restaurants

Bar and restaurant margins are thin enough that a bad two weeks can wipe out a good month. Cash moves fast, daily deposits, vendor payments, payroll, tip payouts, and it's easy to lose sight of where it's actually going until the bank balance tells you something's wrong.

We build cash tracking around how [bars and restaurants](/industries/restaurants) actually operate: daily sales against daily cash out, seasonal swings around holidays and summer patio season, and the timing of liquor and food vendor payments against weekly deposits. That day-to-day visibility is what lets an owner catch a margin problem in week two instead of finding it in the month-end numbers.

When a new client comes on board, Stephen and his team take time to learn how that business actually runs, its billing cycle, its payroll quirks, its busy season, before touching a single spreadsheet. Clients don't get generic advice pulled from a textbook. They get guidance built around how their business actually operates, from someone who took the time to ask first.

## Deep roots in Westchester County and beyond

Port Chester is home base, but the firm's reach extends well past Westchester County. Stephen works with business owners throughout the county, along with clients in Manhattan and Brooklyn who want a CPA who still picks up the phone. The firm also serves clients in Asbury Park, New Jersey, and individuals and business owners across New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Florida.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Specialized experience in construction, real estate, and hospitality

Stephen built his practice around three industries where the accounting gets complicated fast: construction, real estate, and hospitality, with particular depth in bars and pubs.

### Construction
icon: Hammer

Job costing separates a profitable project from one that quietly loses money. Stephen tracks profitability phase by phase, works through payroll complexities tied to certified payroll and job-specific rates, and helps contractors spot cash flow gaps before they become a problem.

### Real Estate
icon: Home

Depreciation strategy and cost segregation can mean the difference between an average tax year and a great one. Stephen works with real estate owners and investors on 1031 exchange timing, entity structuring, and the kind of planning that protects gains instead of handing them to the IRS.

### Bars and Restaurants
icon: Receipt

Thin margins leave no room for guesswork. Stephen helps bar and restaurant owners get a clear read on where money actually goes, stay compliant on tip reporting and cash handling, and untangle sales tax rules that trip up even experienced operators.

### Summer Camps May Qualify for Dependent Care Tax Credit | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/summer-camps-may-qualify-for-dependent-care-tax-credit

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Why summer camp costs can work in your favor at tax time

If you're a working parent in Port Chester or anywhere else in Westchester County, summer camp isn't just a scheduling solution, it's often a legitimate tax break hiding in plain sight. The dependent care tax credit was built for exactly this situation: parents who need supervised care for a child under 13 so they can work, and who pay for it out of pocket. Day camp tuition frequently qualifies, yet plenty of families never claim it because the rules feel murky or they assume camp costs don't count. They often do. A quick conversation with a CPA who knows the details can mean the difference between leaving money on the table and turning a summer expense into a real credit on your return.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: parent-dropping-child-summer-camp.jpg | alt: "Parent dropping off child at a day camp drop-off line" | query: "parent child summer camp drop off" -->
## Which camps and expenses qualify

The IRS draws a firm line here: day camps qualify, overnight camps do not, even if it's the same organization running both programs. The logic is simple. The credit exists to cover care that lets you work during the day, not lodging. Here's a quick self-check before you file:

- The camp operates during the day and does not include overnight stays
- The child is under 13, or is a dependent unable to care for themselves
- The camp expense enabled you (and your spouse, if filing jointly) to work or look for work
- You have the camp provider's name, address, and taxpayer ID number
- Specialty camps count too. Sports, art, coding, and academic day camps generally qualify the same way a traditional day camp does

A common misconception: parents assume only traditional summer camps qualify. In reality, before- and after-school care programs and even summer day programs run by a local YMCA or municipal recreation department can count, as long as the daytime-only rule holds.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How much you could save with the dependent care credit

The math isn't complicated once you see it laid out. You can count up to $3,000 in qualifying expenses for one child, or $6,000 for two or more children, in a given tax year. The credit itself is a percentage of that amount, ranging from 20% to 35% depending on your adjusted gross income, with higher-income households landing at the lower end of that range. In practical terms, that means the credit could put anywhere from $600 to $2,100 back in your pocket for two kids at camp, depending on your income and expenses. It's not a deduction that only shaves a little off taxable income. It's a direct, dollar-for-dollar reduction of what you owe, which is why it's worth getting right. Our [tax planning services](/what-we-do/tax) walk through the calculation using your actual numbers rather than a rough estimate.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: family-reviewing-tax-documents.jpg | alt: "Parents reviewing financial paperwork together at home" | query: "parents reviewing paperwork home" -->
## Dependent care FSA versus the tax credit

Many Westchester County parents have access to a dependent care flexible spending account through their employer, and it raises a fair question: FSA or tax credit, or both? You can use an FSA to set aside up to $5,000 pretax for dependent care, which lowers your taxable income right away. The catch is you can't double-dip. Any camp expenses paid through the FSA can't also be claimed for the credit, and the $3,000/$6,000 expense caps for the credit get reduced by whatever you ran through the FSA. For some families, the FSA wins because it lowers income before payroll taxes even apply. For others, especially those in a lower tax bracket where the credit's percentage runs higher, claiming the credit outright makes more sense. This is a household-by-household calculation, and it's exactly the kind of decision that benefits from sitting down with someone who can run both scenarios side by side.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: filing-receipts-folder.jpg | alt: "Folder of receipts and tax documents organized on a desk" | query: "organized receipts tax documents folder" -->
## Record-keeping tips for Westchester County families

If the IRS ever asks questions, documentation is what settles them quickly and without stress. Keep these on hand throughout the year, not just at tax time:

- Itemized camp receipts or invoices showing dates of attendance and amounts paid
- The camp provider's tax identification number (EIN or Social Security number for an individual provider)
- Proof that both parents worked or were actively job-searching during the camp period
- Bank or credit card statements matching the camp payments, in case a receipt goes missing
- A written note if a camp offers both day and overnight programs, clarifying which portion you're claiming

Good habits here pay off well beyond one tax season. Denise Romano, CPA, and the rest of our team see these questions come up every summer, and having the paperwork organized in advance makes filing faster and audit exposure lower.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: family-consultation-cpa-office.jpg | alt: "Family meeting with a CPA advisor at a desk" | query: "family meeting financial advisor office" -->
## Get help planning your family's tax strategy year-round

Summer camp is one piece of a bigger picture. Between dependent care credits, side income, and the usual questions that come up for households across Port Chester and the wider Westchester County area, year-round planning beats a once-a-year scramble every time. Our [personal income tax](/what-we-do/personal-income-tax) services are built around that idea: personalized support that doesn't disappear after April. If you want a clear answer on whether your camp expenses qualify, or how they fit into your broader tax picture, schedule a consultation and we'll work through it together.

### Why Small Businesses Are Going Bankrupt—and How to Avoid It | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/why-small-businesses-are-going-bankrupt-and-how-to-avoid-it

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Why small businesses fail more often than they should

Most business failures don't start with one bad decision. They build slowly: a slow month here, a missed invoice there, a tax bill that arrives bigger than expected than anyone planned for. By the time an owner notices, the problem has already taken root.

Construction firms run out of cash between draws. Restaurants watch margins evaporate without knowing why. Real estate investors miss deductions that would have kept more money in the business. None of this means the owner did anything wrong. It usually means nobody was watching the numbers closely enough, early enough.

That part is fixable. With the right bookkeeping, payroll, and tax planning in place, the warning signs show up months before they'd ever become a crisis.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: contractor-reviewing-invoices.jpg | alt: "Contractor reviewing invoices and cash flow paperwork on site" | query: "contractor reviewing paperwork construction site" -->
## Cash flow problems that quietly sink businesses

Cash flow is where most small business trouble actually begins, not on a balance sheet nobody reads until tax season. A contractor finishes a project and waits 45 days to get paid, but [payroll](/what-we-do/payroll) and material bills don't wait. A bar owner has a great Friday night and a terrible Tuesday, and the monthly average hides both.

Bookkeeping that's current, not three months behind, is what catches this early. Our [bookkeeping](/what-we-do/bookkeeping) and [cash management](/what-we-do/cash-management) services track money in and money out in real time, so an owner sees a shortfall coming in June instead of discovering it in August. Small gaps are manageable. Gaps nobody sees until they've compounded are what push businesses toward bad borrowing decisions.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Industry-specific risks in construction, real estate, and hospitality

### Construction
icon: Hammer

Job costing errors are the quiet killer here. Without tracking labor, materials, and overhead per project, a contractor can finish a job at a loss and not know it until the next one is already underway. Payroll complexity across union and prevailing-wage jobs adds another layer of risk. See how we support [construction businesses](/industries/construction).

### Real Estate
icon: Home

Missed depreciation and cost segregation opportunities leave real money on the table every year. A 1031 exchange handled incorrectly can trigger an unexpected tax bill that undoes months of planning. These aren't edge cases, they're common mistakes among owners without industry-specific guidance. Learn more about [real estate accounting](/industries/real-estate).

### Bars and Restaurants
icon: Receipt

Thin margins mean there's no room for guessing. Cash handling, tip reporting, and sales tax compliance all carry real exposure, and without visibility into where money actually goes, a busy restaurant can still lose money every month. See our approach for [bars and restaurants](/industries/restaurants).

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: business-owner-reviewing-books.jpg | alt: "Small business owner reviewing financial statements at a desk" | query: "small business owner reviewing financial documents" -->
## The warning signs owners often miss

Bookkeeping that's always a month or two behind. Payroll tax deposits made late, or skipped entirely when cash got tight. No forecast beyond hoping next month is better. A tax return that's a surprise every April instead of something planned for months in advance.

These aren't character flaws. They're what happens when day-to-day operations take over and the books get pushed aside. The trouble is these signs are only obvious in hindsight unless someone is looking at the numbers on a regular schedule.

- Books consistently 60+ days out of date
- Payroll tax deposits made late or missed
- No cash flow forecast beyond the current month
- Tax filings handled reactively instead of planned in advance
- Relying on a bank balance instead of actual profit and loss

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: advisor-reviewing-dashboard.jpg | alt: "Accountant and client reviewing financial dashboard on a laptop" | query: "accountant client reviewing laptop dashboard" -->
## How proactive accounting keeps businesses out of trouble

The businesses that avoid these problems aren't luckier. They have a system that surfaces problems early enough to act. Bookkeeping, [payroll](/what-we-do/payroll), [tax planning](/what-we-do/tax), and advisory support working together, under one fixed monthly fee, means nothing falls through the cracks between services.

Clients see their numbers through a secure online platform updated in real time, not a spreadsheet emailed once a quarter. A contractor can check job profitability mid-project. A restaurant owner can see labor costs creeping up before the next payroll run. A real estate investor can plan a sale around tax consequences instead of discovering them after closing.

This is what [advisory](/services/advisory) support looks like day to day: fewer surprises, more decisions made with real information. For a new venture, getting the [accounting system setup](/what-we-do/accounting-system-setup) right from day one, alongside proper [entity structuring](/what-we-do/business-foundation-services), prevents a lot of the trouble described above before it starts.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: port-chester-business-owner-handshake.jpg | alt: "CPA and small business owner shaking hands after a meeting" | query: "business owner accountant handshake meeting" -->
## Let's make sure this doesn't happen to your business

You don't need to wait for a crisis to get a second set of eyes on your numbers. Whether you're running a job site in Port Chester, managing a bar with tight margins, or building a real estate portfolio across Westchester County, a short conversation can tell you a lot about where you actually stand.

We'll look at what's working, what's not, and what to fix first. No pressure, no long contracts, just a clear read on your finances from Stephen Pryor, Shawn Wilson, and Denise Romano, CPAs who've done this for businesses like yours.

[Schedule a consultation](/contact) and get your numbers working for you instead of against you.

### IRS Increases Foreign Earned Income Tax Breaks | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/irs-increases-foreign-earned-income-tax-breaks

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## What changed with the foreign earned income exclusion

The IRS adjusts the foreign earned income exclusion (FEIE) for inflation nearly every year, and the recent bump matters if you're a U.S. citizen or resident working abroad. The exclusion rose from $126,500 to $130,000, meaning qualifying taxpayers can shield that much more foreign wage or self-employment income from federal tax. Pair that with the foreign housing exclusion, and someone renting an apartment in Lisbon or running a consulting gig out of Singapore has real room to lower taxable income before credits even enter the picture.

For Port Chester and Westchester County residents with a spouse working overseas, a rental property abroad, or a remote contract with an international client, this isn't abstract. It's the difference between a tax bill that reflects your full foreign salary and one that reflects only the portion above the exclusion. The mechanics haven't changed. The dollar amount has, and that's worth revisiting with your CPA before you file.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: passport-tax-documents-desk.jpg | alt: "Passport and tax documents on a desk for expat tax filing" | query: "passport travel documents desk" -->
## Who qualifies for these foreign income tax breaks

Qualifying for the FEIE comes down to passing one of two IRS tests. Neither is complicated once you see how the IRS actually applies them.

- **Physical presence test**: You were physically present in a foreign country (or countries) for at least 330 full days during any 12-month period. Vacation days back in Westchester County count against you, so the math needs to be exact.
- **Bona fide residence test**: You established a genuine, uninterrupted residence in a foreign country for an entire tax year, even if you traveled back to the U.S. occasionally.

We see this most often with clients who split time between a business abroad and family in Port Chester, or small business owners managing international contracts while still filing as New York residents. Which test applies changes your filing strategy, and getting it wrong can mean losing the exclusion entirely.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How the exclusion works alongside foreign tax credits

The FEIE and the foreign tax credit both reduce your U.S. tax bill on foreign income, but you can't apply both to the same dollar. Exclude a chunk of income under the FEIE, and you lose the ability to also claim a credit for foreign taxes paid on that same income. For some taxpayers, especially those in higher-tax countries, the foreign tax credit alone produces a better outcome than the exclusion.

This is a planning decision, not a compliance trap. The right answer depends on your income level, the tax rate in the country where you're working, and whether you have other U.S.-source income that changes your bracket. Running both scenarios before you file, rather than defaulting to whichever form feels familiar, is where the real savings show up.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Common mistakes that cost taxpayers this deduction

Most lost deductions come down to timing and documentation, not eligibility. The mistakes we see most often:

- Miscounting qualifying days for the physical presence test, especially around trips home for holidays
- Filing Form 2555 late or not at all, which forfeits the exclusion for that year
- Assuming excluded wages also escape self-employment tax, which they don't
- Overlooking the foreign housing exclusion or deduction that pairs with the FEIE
- Relying on general tax software that wasn't built to flag foreign income elections

Each of these is fixable with a return that's reviewed by someone who knows what to look for before it's filed, not after a notice arrives.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: cpa-video-call-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA reviewing tax documents during a video consultation with a client" | query: "accountant video call consultation" -->
## Why local, year-round guidance matters for expat and overseas income

Foreign income tax planning doesn't work as a once-a-year exercise. The FEIE, housing exclusions, and foreign tax credit decisions all depend on choices you make throughout the year, not just what you report in April. At Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, personal income tax support runs year-round, delivered through a secure online platform so you can see your numbers and share documents from wherever you're working, whether that's a project in Manhattan or a posting overseas.

Bundled service fees mean you're not paying by the question every time a filing decision comes up mid-year. Clients across Westchester County, and as far as Brooklyn, Asbury Park, and clients in NY, NJ, CT, and FL, rely on that steady access instead of scrambling every tax season. It's a different model than a seasonal storefront preparer who reviews your return once and moves on to the next client in line.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: cpa-consultation-handshake.jpg | alt: "CPA and client shaking hands after a tax planning consultation" | query: "business handshake office meeting" -->
## Talk with a Port Chester CPA about your foreign income situation

Foreign earned income rules reward people who plan ahead and cost the ones who guess. If you're working abroad, managing a rental property overseas, or supporting a family member with international income, a short conversation now can save a lot of second-guessing later. ### Cybersecurity Expert: Why Your Business Needs This One Thing That 62% of Companies Already Have | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/cybersecurity-expert-why-your-business-needs-this-one-thing-that-62-of-companies-already-have

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: financial-data-target.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing sensitive financial data on a computer screen" | query: "accountant reviewing financial data computer" -->
## Your financial data is a bigger target than you think

A recent report found that 62% of companies already use some form of formal cybersecurity protection, which means the remaining 38% are sitting exposed with far more to lose than they realize. If you run a business in Port Chester, your books hold client Social Security numbers, bank account access, payroll files, and vendor payment details. That's a far richer target than a typical retail database.

Most small business owners assume hackers go after big corporations. In reality, smaller companies get targeted precisely because their defenses are thinner. A single compromised email attachment containing a payroll file can expose every employee's personal information in seconds. The risk isn't hypothetical. It's sitting in your inbox and your accounting software right now.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Where construction, real estate, and hospitality businesses are most exposed

### Construction
icon: Hammer

Job-cost data and vendor payment files move between project managers, subcontractors, and accounting constantly. That back-and-forth creates openings for invoice fraud, where a criminal intercepts an email thread and redirects a payment to a fake account before anyone notices.

### Real Estate
icon: Home

Tenant applications, lease files, and closing documents carry Social Security numbers, bank routing details, and signed contracts. A single breached email account tied to a property management system can expose dozens of tenants' financial records at once.

### Bars and Restaurants
icon: Receipt

Point-of-sale systems process card data all night long, and tip and payroll records sit right next to them. Weak POS security or shared logins turn a busy Friday shift into a data exposure event nobody catches until the chargebacks start.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: cpa-data-security-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA and business client discussing data security during an office meeting" | query: "cpa client meeting office discussion" -->
## How working with a security-conscious CPA reduces your risk

Most IT vendors sell firewalls and antivirus software without ever looking at how your payroll actually runs or where your job-cost data lives. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA works inside those systems every week, handling bookkeeping, payroll, and tax data for construction, real estate, and hospitality clients across Westchester County.

That daily proximity to sensitive financial information means data protection isn't a bolt-on service. It's built into how bookkeeping, payroll, and tax work get done. When Stephen, Shawn Wilson, CPA, or Denise Romano, CPA sets up your accounting workflow, they're already thinking about who can see what and where your files actually sit.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: secure-online-platform-dashboard.jpg | alt: "Business owner viewing secure financial dashboard on a laptop" | query: "business owner laptop financial dashboard" -->
## What our secure platform means for your financial data

Email attachments and shared spreadsheets are two of the easiest ways financial data leaks out of a small business. A file sent to the wrong address, or a spreadsheet copied one too many times, can put payroll numbers or bank details in the wrong hands with no way to pull it back.

Our secure online platform replaces that guesswork with one encrypted place for your real-time financial data.

- No more emailing sensitive files back and forth
- Real-time visibility into your numbers without downloading spreadsheets
- Access controls that limit who on your team sees payroll or banking details
- One system tracking bookkeeping, payroll, and tax data instead of five

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: business-owner-security-checklist.jpg | alt: "Small business owner reviewing a security checklist on a tablet" | query: "small business owner checklist tablet" -->
## Simple steps to strengthen your business's financial security

You don't need an IT department to close the biggest gaps. A handful of habits, done consistently, cover most of the risk that catches construction, real estate, and hospitality businesses off guard.

- Use unique, strong passwords for banking and payroll logins, not the same one across every account
- Limit who on your staff can access bank feeds, payroll files, or vendor payment systems
- Review your bank and credit card feeds weekly instead of waiting for month-end
- Vet any software vendor before connecting it to your accounting system
- Turn on two-factor authentication anywhere it's offered, especially for banking and email

### How Small Businesses Can Survive Soaring Oil Prices and Keep Customers | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/how-small-businesses-can-survive-soaring-oil-prices-and-keep-customers

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Why rising fuel costs hit Port Chester small businesses hard

Oil prices don't stay contained to the gas pump. When crude spikes, everything riding on a truck, a delivery route, or a job site generator costs more too. For construction crews in Port Chester, that shows up as pricier lumber deliveries and equipment fuel. For real estate operators, it lands in maintenance contracts and landscaping bids. For bars and restaurants, it's a fuel surcharge tacked onto a food distributor invoice, layered on top of margins that were already thin.

None of this arrives labeled "oil price increase." It hides inside vendor bills, delivery fees, and utility statements until an owner notices margins shrinking without knowing exactly why. That's the moment a CPA who already understands construction, real estate, and hospitality numbers can help spot the pattern before it becomes a crisis.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: reviewing-vendor-contract.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing a supplier contract with a calculator nearby" | query: "small business owner reviewing contract paperwork" -->
## Reviewing pricing and vendor contracts before costs eat your margin

When fuel surcharges start showing up on delivery invoices, guessing isn't a strategy. It takes a structured look at where the money is actually going, line by line.

- Renegotiate delivery schedules and minimum order sizes with suppliers to cut down on trip frequency
- Compare vendor fuel surcharge line items against actual mileage to catch overcharges before they compound
- Adjust menu or service pricing in small, regular steps instead of one jump that drives customers away
- Revisit subcontractor and delivery terms on construction jobs before signing the next phase
- Build fuel surcharge clauses into new contracts so the next spike doesn't erode margin all over again

For a bar or restaurant running on single-digit margins, or a contractor bidding the next phase of a job, this review often finds more room to protect profit than a price increase alone ever would.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: real-time-bookkeeping-dashboard.jpg | alt: "Restaurant owner checking a bookkeeping dashboard on a laptop" | query: "small business owner laptop financial dashboard" -->
## Using real-time bookkeeping to spot cost increases early

Most owners find out about a cost problem three months late, once the books finally close for last quarter. By then the damage is done. Bookkeeping through Pryor CPA runs on a secure online platform built for real-time financial data, not a rearview mirror.

That matters most when a single input cost, like diesel or propane, moves fast. A restaurant owner can watch food delivery fees creep up week over week. A contractor can see equipment fuel costs stack up against a specific job before it's ever billed. Catching the trend while it's happening means there's still margin left to protect, instead of finding out after the quarter has already closed.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: cash-flow-forecast-meeting.jpg | alt: "Small business owner and accountant reviewing a cash flow forecast together" | query: "accountant client reviewing financial forecast" -->
## Cash management strategies to keep operations steady

Fuel spikes rarely arrive on a predictable schedule, which is exactly why cash reserves matter more than any single pricing decision. Cash management means knowing what's coming in and going out weeks ahead, not just what sits in the account today.

For a construction business waiting on a draw between project phases, a fuel spike can turn a tight month into a missed payroll run. For a bar or restaurant carrying inventory and weekly payroll obligations, a cushion built from disciplined cash flow forecasting is the difference between absorbing a bad month and scrambling for a short-term loan. Building that forecast, and the reserve to match it, is where cash management planning earns its keep.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Tax planning moves that offset higher operating expenses

Rising costs squeeze margins, and squeezed margins often push owners to stop thinking about taxes until March. That's exactly backward. Quarterly tax planning and projections surface the deductions available for higher fuel, equipment, and delivery costs while there's still time to act on them, not after the year closes.

Higher operating expenses can also mean estimated tax payments need adjusting. Overpaying quarterly estimates during a thin-margin year ties up cash needed for payroll or inventory. Underpaying adds a penalty on top of an already hard year. A CPA reviewing your numbers year-round, not just at filing season, catches both problems before either one costs you.

### Tax Breaks for Data Centers Are On the Chopping Block in Some States | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/tax-breaks-for-data-centers-are-on-the-chopping-block

## States are reconsidering data center tax incentives

A handful of states are pulling back on the tax breaks they once handed data center operators, and the reasoning is straightforward: the credits cost more than lawmakers expected, and the jobs promised didn't always show up. New York hasn't been immune to this kind of reversal. Sales tax exemptions and property tax abatements tied to data centers are getting a second look in several statehouses this year.

The bigger story here isn't about server farms. It's about how quickly a tax incentive that looked permanent can disappear. Business owners who built a tax strategy around a specific credit, exemption, or abatement need someone checking whether that benefit still exists next filing season, not just this one.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: legislative-tax-review.jpg | alt: "Person reviewing state tax legislation documents at a desk" | query: "person reading legal documents office" -->
## Construction, real estate, and hospitality owners feel these shifts too

Data centers aren't the only businesses that lean on state and local incentives. Construction firms in Westchester County often factor in depreciation schedules and project-based credits when bidding jobs. Real estate owners plan around 1031 exchanges and cost segregation studies. Bars and restaurants count on payroll tax credits tied to hiring and, in some states, tip reporting relief.

When legislators revisit one industry's tax breaks, it's usually a signal they're reviewing the whole incentive structure. A property tax abatement your construction company relies on, or a sales tax exemption your restaurant counts on, can get quietly narrowed or sunset in the same budget cycle. If nobody's watching the calendar, you find out when the bill lands, not before.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: construction-real-estate-planning.jpg | alt: "Construction and real estate professionals reviewing financial documents together" | query: "construction real estate business meeting" -->
## How construction and real estate businesses can stay ahead of changing tax rules

Entity structure decisions made five years ago don't always hold up once tax law shifts. A construction company organized as an S-corp might benefit from a different structure once New York adjusts depreciation rules or project-based credits. Real estate owners face similar exposure: cost segregation opportunities and 1031 exchange rules change enough that a plan built in 2022 can leave money on the table in 2026.

Our entity type analysis and ongoing advisory work exist for exactly this reason. We review entity structure, depreciation strategy, and applicable New York incentives on a recurring basis, not once at onboarding. That's how a construction client avoids overpaying because nobody flagged a new state credit, and how a real estate owner catches a cost segregation opportunity before the filing deadline instead of after.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: bar-restaurant-owner-tablet.jpg | alt: "Restaurant owner checking financial data on a tablet behind the bar" | query: "restaurant owner tablet bar" -->
## What this means for bars, restaurants, and other local businesses

Bars and restaurants run on thin margins, and the tax rules that touch them move often: sales tax on prepared food, tip credit reporting, payroll-based hiring incentives. A change in any one of these can shift a bar's monthly numbers more than owners expect, especially when cash handling and tip reporting already demand close attention.

Year-round planning catches these shifts as they happen. Instead of finding out at tax time that a sales tax rule changed six months earlier, a hospitality client gets a heads-up when it's still useful. That's the difference between adjusting pricing or staffing proactively and scrambling to cover a surprise liability in April.

## The value of year-round tax planning over one-time filing

An annual tax return tells you what already happened. It doesn't tell you that a state incentive shifted in March, or that your entity structure stopped making sense after a change in New York's tax code. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, Shawn Wilson, CPA, and Denise Romano, CPA work with clients throughout the year, not just at filing season, so changes like these get flagged when there's still time to act.

### Indiana Adopts No Tax on Tips, Overtime Only for 2026 Tax Year | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/indiana-adopts-no-tax-on-tips-overtime-only-for-2026-tax-year

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## What Indiana's new law changes for 2026

Indiana just passed a law exempting tip income and overtime pay from state income tax, effective with the 2026 tax year. It's a narrower move than the federal "no tax on tips" proposals that circulated in Washington: Indiana's exemption applies only at the state level, and only to those two specific categories of income. Servers, bartenders, and hourly staff who earn overtime in Indiana will see a difference in their state withholding once the law takes effect.

For most business owners outside Indiana, this reads like a small regional headline. It isn't. State legislatures watch each other closely, and tip and overtime taxation has become one of the more active areas of state tax policy over the past two years. If you run a bar, restaurant, or any business with tipped or hourly staff in New York, New Jersey, or Connecticut, this is worth five minutes of your attention.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: hospitality-payroll-review.jpg | alt: "Restaurant manager reviewing payroll and tip reports on a laptop" | query: "restaurant manager reviewing payroll laptop" -->
## Why this matters even outside Indiana

State tax rules on tips and overtime don't move in isolation. When one state changes how it treats tipped wages, other states tend to face pressure, either from workforce competition or from legislators pointing to it as a model. New York, New Jersey, and Connecticut all have their own tip credit rules, overtime thresholds, and reporting requirements already, and none of them mirror each other exactly.

For a bar or restaurant owner in Port Chester, that patchwork is the real issue. You might employ staff who live in Connecticut, run payroll under New York wage and hour rules, and watch federal proposals shift the ground again. Each layer changes independently. Indiana's move is a signal that tip and overtime taxation is unsettled territory right now, not a one-time headline. Owners who track these changes as they happen have more room to adjust withholding, staffing costs, and pricing before a rule catches them off guard rather than after.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: bartender-pos-tip-reporting.jpg | alt: "Bartender entering tip totals into a point of sale system" | query: "bartender entering data point of sale" -->
## Tip income and overtime reporting complexity for hospitality employers

Tip and overtime rules create more day-to-day payroll work than most owners expect, especially once a business operates in more than one state or has staff who split time between tipped and non-tipped duties. The parts that tend to trip owners up include:

- Calculating the correct tip credit against minimum wage under state-specific rules
- Reconciling reported tips against credit card and POS tip data for accuracy
- Tracking overtime for employees whose pay includes both a base wage and tips
- Filing payroll taxes correctly across multiple states or locations
- Keeping W-2 and 1099 reporting consistent with actual tip income received

We handle payroll processing and filings for bars, restaurants, and hospitality clients across Westchester County, and tip reporting compliance is one of the most common places we find errors during onboarding. A missed tip credit calculation or an inconsistent filing across two locations can turn into a bigger problem at tax time, which is exactly the kind of gap our [payroll services](/what-we-do/payroll) are built to close.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: business-owner-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Business owner and accountant reviewing tax planning documents together" | query: "business owner accountant tax planning meeting" -->
## How Port Chester and Westchester business owners can stay ahead of tax law changes

Legislative shifts like Indiana's rarely arrive with much warning, and by the time a change is finalized, business owners are often reacting instead of planning. Year-round tax planning is the difference between the two. Instead of waiting for filing season to find out what changed, you get a running conversation with your CPA about what's coming, what applies to your business, and what to adjust now.

Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, and the firm's team of CPAs, including Shawn Wilson and Denise Romano, work with construction, real estate, and hospitality clients throughout Westchester County, Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Asbury Park, NJ, to keep tax planning and projections current as rules shift. That means fewer surprises at year-end and more time to make decisions, like adjusting payroll systems or staffing costs, while there's still room to act. It's part of why clients come to us for [tax planning and preparation](/what-we-do/tax) rather than treating it as a once-a-year task.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: port-chester-hospitality-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA and restaurant owner discussing tax and payroll strategy in an office" | query: "accountant restaurant owner discussing strategy" -->

### IRS Gives Taxpayers a More Streamlined Way to Report Tax Fraud and Scams | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/quick-reads/irs-gives-taxpayers-new-way-to-report-tax-fraud

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## IRS rolls out a simpler way to report tax fraud and scams

The IRS recently streamlined how taxpayers and business owners report suspected fraud, phishing attempts, and tax scams. Instead of sorting through a maze of forms to figure out where a complaint belongs, filers now have a more direct channel for flagging suspicious activity, whether that's a fake charity solicitation, a text message posing as the IRS, or a preparer inflating deductions without your knowledge.

For business owners in Port Chester, NY, this update lands at a useful time. Tax season brings a predictable wave of scam attempts aimed at construction crews, restaurant staff, and property managers alike. A faster reporting path means less time spent figuring out who to call and more time getting a fraudulent notice or scam text in front of the right people. [Stephen P. Pryor, CPA](/who-we-are/stephen-pryor) tracks changes like this one so Westchester County clients don't have to.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Why tax fraud and scam awareness matters for local businesses and individuals

[Construction companies](/industries/construction) juggling multiple subcontractors face a specific kind of exposure: fake W-9 requests, inflated invoices, and payroll scams that mimic a real vendor's email address down to the letter. [Real estate businesses](/industries/real-estate) handling closings and 1031 exchanges are frequent targets for wire fraud schemes that impersonate title companies or the IRS itself. [Bars and restaurants](/industries/restaurants), with cash-heavy operations and tip reporting already under scrutiny, see a steady stream of phishing attempts aimed squarely at bookkeepers and payroll staff.

None of this is unique to Manhattan or Brooklyn. Port Chester and the surrounding Westchester County business community see the same scam patterns, just with fewer resources aimed at catching them early. A restaurant manager who wires money based on a spoofed email, or a contractor who pays a fake subcontractor invoice, loses real cash with little chance of getting it back. Awareness is the cheapest protection a business has.

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: vertical -->
## What to do if you suspect fraud or receive a suspicious notice

### Verify before you respond
The IRS does not initiate contact by text, email, or social media asking for payment. A phone call to a number you look up independently, not one printed on the suspicious notice, is the safest first move.

### Document everything
Save the email, screenshot the text, and keep the notice itself. Details like sender addresses and dates matter if you need to file a report later.

### Report it to the right place
Suspicious IRS-related activity gets reported directly to the IRS through its updated reporting channel. Scams involving your bank or payroll provider should also go to them directly.

### Call your CPA before you act
Before wiring money, replying to a notice, or changing payroll information based on an email request, get a second set of eyes on it. A quick call can save you from an expensive mistake.

<!-- block: content-prose -->

Pryor, CPA](/who-we-are/stephen-pryor) handles your [bookkeeping and payroll](/services/bookkeeping) each month, unusual transactions surface within weeks instead of sitting unnoticed for a full year. Clients on the firm's bundled monthly service get real-time visibility into their accounts through a secure online platform, so a fraudulent charge or payroll discrepancy gets flagged fast, not discovered at tax time.

Year-round [tax planning](/services/tax) plays a role too. When [Shawn Wilson, CPA](/who-we-are/shawn-wilson) or [Denise Romano, CPA](/who-we-are/denise-romano) reviews your numbers on an ongoing basis rather than once a year, they know what your filings should look like. That makes it far easier to spot a fraudulent notice that doesn't match your actual account history. For a deeper look at protecting your records, the firm's [guide on safeguarding financial data](/resources/e-books/protecting-your-financial-data-a-small-business-owner-s-guide) walks through the basics.

A busy month meant a bigger bill, even though nothing about the work actually changed. Hourly billing puts the risk on you, the client, and that's backwards.

Subscription pricing flips that arrangement. You pay one flat amount every month for bookkeeping, payroll, tax, and advisory work, and that number doesn't move just because your business had a busy quarter. Stephen P. Pryor, CPA built this model because clients kept asking for the same thing: a number they could plan around.

### Cybersecurity on a shoestring budget | Stephen P. Pryor, CPA
URL: /resources/e-books/cybersecurity-on-a-shoestring-budget

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Why small businesses in Port Chester are prime cybersecurity targets

Ask any restaurant owner in Port Chester whether hackers are interested in a business with a dozen employees and a single register, and most will laugh off the idea. That assumption is exactly what makes construction firms, real estate offices, and neighborhood bars such reliable targets. Cyber criminals don't chase size, they chase gaps: no dedicated IT staff, shared logins, and point-of-sale systems nobody has updated since 2019. Small operators in Westchester County rarely have the cash reserves to absorb a six-figure recovery bill, which is what separates a bad week from a business-ending one. This isn't a problem for your IT guy to solve later. A breach touches payroll, vendor payments, and tax filings, which makes it a financial risk first and a technical one second. Treating cybersecurity like a bookkeeping line item, something you budget for and review regularly, is the more realistic approach for a construction crew or a two-location restaurant group.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: cpa-reviewing-financial-security.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing financial records on a laptop with a client" | query: "accountant reviewing financial documents laptop" -->
## The financial and tax risks of a data breach

A data breach rarely stays contained to a computer screen. Once payroll files, bank account numbers, or client W-9s are exposed, you're looking at fraudulent tax filings, unauthorized wire transfers, and clients who no longer trust you with their financial details. For a construction company juggling subcontractor payments or a bar owner processing nightly credit card batches, that exposure compounds fast. This is where a CPA who already knows your [bookkeeping](/what-we-do/bookkeeping) and [payroll](/what-we-do/payroll) systems has an edge over a generic IT vendor. Stephen Pryor, Shawn Wilson, and Denise Romano review client books closely enough to notice when a vendor invoice looks off, a payroll run doesn't match hours logged, or a bank reconciliation turns up a transaction nobody recognizes. Catching those anomalies early is often what keeps a security incident from becoming a tax problem too.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: small-business-owner-security-checklist.jpg | alt: "Small business owner checking cybersecurity tasks on a tablet" | query: "small business owner using tablet office" -->
## Low cost cybersecurity steps any business owner can take today

You don't need a six-figure IT budget to close the gaps that hackers exploit most. Most of these steps cost nothing beyond the time it takes to set them up, and they work whether you're running a two-person real estate office or a restaurant with a dozen part-time servers.

- Use a password manager so employees stop reusing the same login across your point-of-sale system, email, and bank accounts.
- Turn on two-factor authentication for banking, payroll, and email logins; it stops most stolen-password attacks cold.
- Set software and point-of-sale systems to update automatically instead of waiting for a "later" that never comes.
- Train employees on spotting phishing emails during onboarding, and again once a year, not just once.
- Back up financial records and job files to a second location, whether that's cloud storage or an external drive kept off-site.
- Limit who can access payroll and banking logins to the people who actually need them.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Industry-specific risks for construction, real estate, and restaurant businesses

### Construction
icon: Hammer

Job-site laptops and tablets often connect to public Wi-Fi at multiple locations, and subcontractor payment details get shared over email without a second thought. A lost device or a spoofed invoice email can drain a project's cash flow before a job costing report even catches it. See how we support [construction businesses](/industries/construction) day to day.

### Real Estate
icon: Home

Real estate offices store closing documents, social security numbers, and wire instructions, exactly the data wire fraud schemes target. A single spoofed email asking a buyer to "update" wiring instructions has cost firms hundreds of thousands of dollars. Our work with [real estate clients](/industries/real-estate) includes flagging these exposure points during onboarding.

### Bars and Restaurants
icon: Wallet

Point-of-sale systems and tip reporting create a steady flow of card data and cash handling records, both attractive to thieves and both subject to compliance rules. Outdated POS software is one of the most common entry points for restaurant breaches. See how we work with [restaurant and bar owners](/industries/restaurants) on this.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: secure-client-portal-dashboard.jpg | alt: "Business owner viewing financial dashboard on a secure online portal" | query: "person viewing dashboard laptop screen" -->
## How working with a CPA who uses a secure platform protects your data

Every bookkeeping entry, payroll run, and tax document you send us moves through a secure online platform built for real-time financial data, not email attachments sitting in an inbox indefinitely. That matters because email is still the easiest way for financial data to leak, whether through a hacked account or a simple misdirected message. When your numbers live in one protected system instead of scattered across spreadsheets and old emails, there's less surface area for something to go wrong. This is part of why bundled [bookkeeping](/what-we-do/bookkeeping), [payroll](/what-we-do/payroll), and [advisory](/services/advisory) services for a fixed monthly fee include more than convenience. Personalized, year-round support means someone is actually looking at your accounts, not just processing them once a year at tax time.
