### Keeping a Balanced Investment Portfolio: A CPA's Guide
URL: /resources/strategically-balancing-your-investment-portfolio-why-set-it

A slow cooker rewards you for walking away. A stock portfolio doesn't. Leave a 401(k) or brokerage account untouched for five years and the mix of stocks, bonds, and cash you started with stops being the mix you actually have. One sector runs hot, another stalls, and by the time you glance at a statement, a portfolio built for moderate risk has quietly turned aggressive. That drift is the real cost of set-it-and-forget-it investing. It doesn't show up as a bill you can see. It shows up as risk you never agreed to.

For business owners in Port Chester and across Westchester County, this matters more than it might seem. Most people in their 40s and 50s aren't checking their asset allocation strategy every quarter. They're running a restaurant, managing a construction crew, or closing on a rental property. Investments sit in the background until a life event, a market swing, or a tax return forces a second look. By then, the portfolio has usually drifted further than anyone realized.

## Why your portfolio drifts even when you never touch it

Say you built a 70% stocks, 30% bonds portfolio in 2019 because that felt like the right risk level at the time. Stocks have a strong run over the next five years while bonds trade sideways. Without a single trade, that 70/30 split can quietly become 82/18. Nobody decided to take on more risk. The market decided for you.

This is the part most people miss about portfolio rebalancing: it's not about picking better investments. It's about periodically resetting the mix back to what you actually intended, so a good run in one asset class doesn't accidentally concentrate your risk. Left alone, winners keep growing as a share of the portfolio and losers keep shrinking, until the account no longer reflects the risk tolerance you started with.

## Your risk tolerance changes even if your portfolio doesn't

Risk tolerance investing isn't a one-time questionnaire you fill out when you open an account. It shifts with your life. A 38-year-old building a bar and grill with three years of runway left on a loan can absorb more volatility than a 58-year-old who just sold that same business and is living off the proceeds. A new rental property purchase changes your liquidity needs. A child heading to college in two years changes your time horizon.

The Federal Reserve's research on household finance and investment behavior points to something worth sitting with: household decisions around saving and investing often lag real changes in financial circumstances by years, not months (see the [Federal Reserve's Notes on Household Finance and Investment Behavior](https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/default.htm)). People keep investing the way they did five years ago because that's the plan they set up, not because it still fits. A portfolio that made sense when you were building your business doesn't automatically make sense once the business is stable, sold, or handed to a partner.

## Rebalancing triggers a tax bill if you don't plan for it

Here's where a lot of DIY rebalancing goes wrong. Selling appreciated stock to bring an allocation back in line feels like housekeeping, but in a taxable brokerage account, it's a taxable event. Sell a position you've held for over a year and you owe long-term capital gains tax. Sell something held less than a year, and it's taxed as ordinary income, often a much bigger hit.

There are ways around this that most people never use because nobody tells them:

- Rebalance inside a 401(k) or IRA first, where trades don't trigger a current tax bill.
- Direct new contributions toward the underweighted asset class instead of selling the overweighted one.
- Pair gains with tax-loss harvesting elsewhere in the portfolio in the same calendar year.
- Time larger rebalancing trades around a lower-income year, if one is coming.

This is exactly the kind of decision that belongs in a year-round tax planning conversation, not a scramble every April. Our [tax services](/services/tax) build rebalancing timing into the broader tax picture for clients throughout the year, not just at filing season.

## Diversification and asset allocation solve different problems

People use portfolio diversification and asset allocation interchangeably, but they answer different questions. Asset allocation is the big-picture split, stocks versus bonds versus cash versus real estate. Diversification is what happens inside each of those buckets, so a downturn in one company, sector, or property doesn't take the whole portfolio down with it.

This gets more complicated for clients who already have real estate exposure through their business or personal holdings. If you own a rental property in Rye or Mamaroneck alongside a brokerage account, that property is part of your overall allocation, whether you think of it that way or not. A portfolio that looks diversified on a Schwab statement can still be overweighted in real estate once you count the rental income, the equity, and the mortgage risk sitting outside the brokerage entirely.

| Concept | What it controls | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Asset allocation | Overall mix of asset classes | 60% stocks, 30% bonds, 10% real estate |
| Diversification | Spread within an asset class | 15 stocks across 6 sectors instead of 3 tech stocks |

## Where your CPA fits into the rebalancing conversation

A CPA doesn't pick your stocks. That's not the job, and Stephen P. Pryor, CPA, doesn't pretend otherwise. What a CPA does well is the tax side of the decision: when a rebalancing trade makes sense given your bracket this year, how a sale interacts with your business income, and what a rental property sale or 1031 exchange does to the rest of your allocation. Stephen Pryor, Shawn Wilson, CPA, and Denise Romano, CPA, work through these questions with clients as part of the same year-round advisory relationship that covers bookkeeping, payroll, and tax.

The AICPA's personal financial planning resources describe this coordination well: a CPA who understands your full tax picture is often better positioned to catch the cost of a badly timed trade than an advisor who only sees the investment account (see the [AICPA Personal Financial Planning resources](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/topic/personal-financial-planning)). That's the gap our [advisory services](/services/advisory) are built to close, especially for construction, real estate, and hospitality business owners whose personal and business finances are more intertwined than a standard financial plan usually accounts for.

Clients working with our firm get access to a secure online platform showing real-time financial data, so a conversation about rebalancing doesn't start with three weeks of pulling statements together. It starts with the numbers already in front of both of you.

## Common Questions

**How often should I rebalance my portfolio?**
Most financial professionals suggest reviewing allocation at least once a year, or any time one asset class drifts more than 5 to 10 percentage points from its target. The right frequency depends on how volatile your holdings are and how much new money you're adding regularly.

**Does rebalancing always trigger capital gains tax?**
Only in taxable accounts. Rebalancing inside a 401(k), IRA, or Roth account doesn't create a current tax bill. In a taxable brokerage account, selling appreciated positions to rebalance does trigger gains, which is why timing and tax-loss harvesting matter.

**What's the real difference between diversification and asset allocation?**
Asset allocation is your split across major categories like stocks, bonds, cash, and real estate. Diversification is how spread out your holdings are within each of those categories. You can have a diversified stock portfolio that's still badly allocated if it's 90% of your net worth.

**Can a CPA help me rebalance, or do I need a financial advisor?**
Both roles matter, and they're not interchangeable. A financial advisor typically handles the trades and investment selection. A CPA handles the tax consequences of those trades and how they fit into your broader tax planning, business income, and year-end strategy.

If your portfolio hasn't had a real review in a while, or if a business sale, property purchase, or retirement is coming up, that's the moment allocation and tax planning need to be looked at together, not separately. [Contact Stephen P. Pryor, CPA](/contact) to talk through what a coordinated review would look like for your specific situation.

### Your Money Mindset Is Costing Your Small Business More Than Your Budget
URL: /resources/your-money-mindset-is-costing-your-small-business-more-than

You can have flawless books and still feel like you're white-knuckling every deposit. That's the part most small business owners never say out loud: the numbers can be accurate and the anxiety can still be there. A contractor in Port Chester might reconcile every invoice on time and still underbid the next job because he's afraid of losing it. A bar owner might know her pour cost down to the penny and still refuse to raise the price of a draft because she's scared regulars will walk. The spreadsheet isn't lying. The decision-making around it is.

This is the piece that gets skipped. Business owners fix the bookkeeping, hire someone for payroll, maybe bring in a CPA for taxes, and assume the financial picture will straighten itself out. Often it doesn't, because the same pricing hesitation, the same avoidance, and the same last-minute tax scramble happen again the next year. The books changed. The behavior around money didn't.

## The pattern repeats because the trigger never gets addressed

Most owners we work with in construction, real estate, and hospitality can describe their own cycle without much prompting. A general contractor quotes low to win the bid, then absorbs the cost overruns because job costing was never tracked project by project. A landlord skips the monthly reconciliation because looking at the numbers feels like inviting bad news. A restaurant owner delays raising menu prices for two years while food costs climb, then panics and raises everything at once, losing regulars who feel blindsided.

None of these are math errors. They're decisions made under stress, repeated because nothing interrupted the pattern. The [AICPA's small business resources](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/resources/landing/small-business-resources) point to the same root issue across industries: owners who treat financial review as a once-a-year event, rather than a habit, make reactive decisions instead of informed ones.

## Underpricing feels safe until it costs you the year

A bar with a 22% pour cost and a $6 draft price is barely breaking even on beer once rent, payroll, and insurance climb. We've seen owners hold that price for three straight years because they're afraid of the conversation with regulars, while their real cost of doing business rose 8% or more. The fear is understandable. The math doesn't care.

Construction has its own version. A contractor who bids tight to beat a competitor is making a psychological bet, not a financial one: that volume will cover the gap somewhere down the line. It rarely does, especially without job costing broken out by project. Without that visibility, a business can look busy and still be losing money on half its jobs. That's not a pricing strategy. It's avoidance wearing a business plan's clothes.

## Avoiding the financial statements doesn't protect you from what's in them

There's a specific kind of dread that keeps owners from opening their profit and loss statement in January. Skipping it doesn't make the number better. It just delays the moment you find out, usually at the worst time, like right before a tax deadline or a loan application.

Real estate owners run into this constantly with depreciation. A landlord who never sits down with a CPA to review cost recovery options can miss a cost segregation study that would have accelerated depreciation by tens of thousands of dollars in year one. We break this down in more detail in [our piece on cost segregation studies](/resources/cost-segregation-studies-are-a-construction-companys-most-ov), and the short version is this: the opportunity doesn't announce itself. You have to be looking.

The fix isn't complicated, but it does require a habit shift. Reviewing a profit and loss statement and balance sheet monthly, even for fifteen minutes, changes the relationship an owner has with the numbers. It stops being a report card and starts being a dashboard. If reading those statements feels intimidating, our [guide to reading a financial statement](/resources/e-books/how-to-read-a-financial-statement) walks through exactly what each line means and why it matters for decisions you're already making.

## Reactive tax decisions cost more than the tax bill itself

Waiting until March to think about taxes is one of the most expensive habits a business owner can carry, and it's rarely about laziness. It's about avoidance. Facing a tax bill feels like facing a verdict, so many owners put it off until there's no room left to plan.

By the time a return is due, most of the moves that actually reduce a tax bill, entity structure, retirement plan contributions, timing of equipment purchases, are already off the table. The [SBA's guide to managing your finances](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/manage-your-business/manage-your-finances) puts it plainly: financial planning works best as an ongoing practice, not a once-a-year scramble. A hospitality business dealing with tip reporting and sales tax complexity, or a construction company managing payroll across multiple job sites, has even less room for a reactive approach. Quarterly check-ins catch problems while there's still time to act on them.

## Small shifts that change the numbers, not just the mood

The fix isn't a mindset seminar. It's structural. Owners who break the cycle usually do three things differently: they look at their numbers on a set schedule instead of when panic sets in, they price based on actual cost data instead of gut feel, and they bring in outside expertise before a decision instead of after a mistake.

Stephen Pryor, CPA, along with Shawn Wilson, CPA, and Denise Romano, CPA, built this firm around exactly that kind of steady, year-round involvement rather than a once-a-year tax appointment. Clients get bundled bookkeeping, payroll, tax, and [advisory support](/services/advisory) for one fixed monthly fee, with access to a secure online platform that shows real financial data whenever they want to look, not just when a report is finally finished. That access alone changes behavior. An owner who can check cash position on a Tuesday afternoon is far less likely to make a decision out of fear on a Friday.

For a [restaurant or bar owner](/industries/restaurants) watching margins tighten, that means seeing pour cost and labor cost trends before they become a crisis. For a [construction business](/industries/construction), it means job costing that shows profitability project by project, not just at year-end. The numbers don't change on their own. The habit of looking at them, consistently and without dread, is what actually moves the needle.

If you want a shorter, more tactical starting point, our earlier post on [building a healthy money mindset](/resources/quick-reads/5-tips-to-build-a-healthy-money-mindset-and-grow-your-finances) covers five habits you can start this month without overhauling your whole system.

## Common Questions

**What is a money mindset for a small business owner?**
It's the set of beliefs and habits that shape financial decisions, like pricing, spending, and avoidance of financial review, separate from whether the bookkeeping itself is accurate. Two businesses with identical books can make very different decisions depending on the owner's comfort with looking at and acting on the numbers.

**Why do small business owners avoid looking at their financial statements?**
Usually because the statements feel like a verdict rather than a tool. Owners who only look at their numbers during tax season tend to associate financial review with stress, which reinforces the avoidance. Monthly review, even brief, breaks that association over time.

**How does underpricing connect to financial psychology rather than just math?**
Underpricing often comes from fear, of losing a customer, a bid, or a regular, rather than from a miscalculation. A contractor or bar owner can know their true costs and still hold prices too low because raising them feels riskier than absorbing the loss. Reviewing actual job costs or pour costs regularly makes the pricing decision fact-based instead of fear-based.

**Can a CPA firm actually help with financial mindset, not just tax filing?**
Yes. A CPA who reviews your numbers year-round, rather than once a year, can flag patterns like chronic underpricing or reactive tax decisions before they compound. That kind of ongoing involvement, paired with real-time access to your financial data, is what turns a mindset conversation into an actual change in the numbers.

If the same cash flow stress or pricing hesitation has shown up again this year, it's worth a conversation before the pattern repeats a third time. [Contact Stephen P. Pryor, CPA](/contact) to talk through what's actually driving the numbers, not just what they say.

### Cost Segregation Studies Are a Construction Company's Most Overlooked Tax Weapon
URL: /resources/cost-segregation-studies-are-a-construction-companys-most-ov

A construction company finishes out a 40,000-square-foot warehouse for a client, then turns around and builds its own equipment yard and office three towns over. Nobody on that job stops to ask whether the electrical subpanels, the specialty flooring, or the site lighting really belong in a 39-year tax life or something much shorter. That question is a cost segregation study, and for construction companies, skipping it is one of the more expensive mistakes we see at our Port Chester office.

Most owners hear "cost segregation" and assume it's a real estate investor's tool, something for someone buying an apartment building or a strip mall. That assumption costs contractors real money every year.

## Real estate investors didn't invent this, they just talk about it more

Cost segregation studies break a building's cost into components with different depreciation lives under IRS rules: the structure itself over 39 years (or 27.5 for residential), but electrical work tied to specific equipment, certain plumbing, carpeting, cabinetry, parking lot paving, and landscaping often qualify for 5-, 7-, or 15-year lives instead. Real estate investors use this constantly because they buy finished buildings and want faster depreciation.

Construction companies are arguably better positioned to benefit. You're not buying a finished building from someone else and guessing at costs after the fact. You're constantly building, expanding, or buying facilities for your own operations, and you often self-perform the very work that creates the best reclassification opportunities. A general contractor who builds out a new shop, a specialty subcontractor who buys a warehouse for staging and storage, a paving company that constructs its own equipment yard: each of these is a cost segregation candidate that rarely gets the study done.

## Your job costing records are already halfway to the study

Here's the part most owners miss. A cost segregation study built by an engineering firm typically starts by reconstructing costs component by component, which is expensive and slow when the building was bought from someone else with no detailed records. Construction companies don't have that problem. If you self-performed part of the work, your own job costing system already tracks labor and materials by trade, by phase, by cost code.

That existing documentation makes the study faster, often cheaper, and considerably more defensible if the IRS ever asks questions. An engineer reviewing your project can point to your own invoices and time records for the electrical subcontractor, the specialty concrete work, or the site utilities, rather than estimating backward from a purchase price. Contractors who already deal with job costing complexity across multiple projects are sitting on the exact records that make this strategy work well.

## The building components that move from 39 years to 5

A typical study on a commercial or light industrial building reclassifies somewhere between 15% and 35% of total building cost into shorter recovery periods, depending on the type of facility. For construction companies building shops, yards, and offices, the categories usually include:

| Component | Standard life | Reclassified life |
|---|---|---|
| Structural shell, roof, foundation | 39 years | Stays at 39 years |
| Dedicated electrical for equipment | 39 years | 5 or 7 years |
| Specialty flooring, certain interior finishes | 39 years | 7 or 15 years |
| Parking lots, curbing, site lighting | 39 years | 15 years |
| Fencing, landscaping | 39 years | 15 years |

The categories that move to 5- and 7-year lives are the ones worth the most attention, because those are the assets that qualify for bonus depreciation right now, not just faster depreciation over time.

## Bonus depreciation is shrinking, which makes timing urgent

Bonus depreciation let businesses write off 100% of qualifying short-life property in the year it was placed in service through 2022. That percentage dropped to 80% in 2023, 60% in 2024, and sits at 40% for property placed in service in 2025. It's scheduled to fall to 20% in 2026 and disappear in 2027 unless Congress changes course again.

Every year a construction company waits to identify its 5- and 7-year property is a year that same property qualifies for a smaller bonus percentage. A facility placed in service in 2024 captured 60% bonus on reclassified assets. The identical building placed in service in 2026 captures 20%. The tax law didn't change what qualifies. It changed how much of it you get to deduct immediately, and that window is closing on a fixed schedule.

## A rough number to make this concrete

Say a contractor buys and renovates a $1.5 million facility for its own equipment storage and office use, excluding land value. A study identifies 22% of that cost, roughly $330,000, as 5-, 7-, or 15-year property instead of 39-year property. At 40% bonus depreciation, that's a first-year deduction of about $132,000 on the reclassified assets alone, on top of standard depreciation on the rest of the building.

Compare that to depreciating the entire $1.5 million evenly over 39 years, which produces roughly $38,000 a year regardless of what's actually inside the walls. For a construction company already dealing with thin margins between project phases and uneven cash flow, that gap between $132,000 and $38,000 in year one is the kind of number that changes what's possible with equipment purchases, hiring, or paying down debt.

## Where this fits into your broader tax plan

Cost segregation isn't a one-time trick you run and forget. It works best as part of a year-round plan that also looks at entity structure, retirement plan options, and how project timing affects your effective tax rate. Stephen Pryor, CPA, Shawn Wilson, CPA, and Denise Romano, CPA work with construction and real estate clients throughout Westchester County on exactly this kind of planning, not just at tax season but when a purchase or build-out decision is still on the table, which is when the study actually has room to help.

The firm's [construction industry services](/industries/construction) are built around the specific pain points contractors deal with: job costing complexity, payroll across multiple projects, and cash flow that swings hard between phases. Cost segregation studies fit naturally alongside [year-round tax planning](/services/tax) rather than as a separate, occasional favor. If you want a broader look at how proactive planning affects what you keep, the firm's guide on [tax planning strategies](/resources/e-books/maximizing-your-tax-refund-a-strategic-guide-to-tax-planning) walks through the same mindset applied to individual and business returns.

## Common Questions

**Does a cost segregation study only apply to buildings I own, or can it apply to a building I lease and improve?**
It generally applies to buildings you own or to leasehold improvements you pay for and capitalize, even if you don't own the underlying real estate. If your construction company built out a leased shop or office and paid for those improvements directly, that cost may still qualify for a study.

**How much does a cost segregation study cost, and is it worth it for a smaller facility?**
Studies typically run a few thousand dollars into the low tens of thousands depending on building size and complexity, and they usually make sense once building costs (excluding land) exceed roughly $500,000. Below that, the tax savings may not outweigh the study cost, though it's worth running the numbers on a specific project rather than assuming.

**Will a cost segregation study increase my audit risk?**
A properly documented, engineering-based study is a standard, IRS-recognized method, not a red flag by itself. The risk comes from sloppy or unsupported studies, which is exactly why using your own detailed job costing records as backup matters so much for construction companies specifically.

**Can I do a cost segregation study on a building I bought or built years ago?**
Yes, through a process called a look-back study, which lets you claim the missed depreciation in the current year without amending prior returns. It's worth reviewing any building placed in service in the last several years that never went through this process.

If your company has built, bought, or renovated a facility in the last few years and never looked at cost segregation, it's worth a conversation before your next tax filing rather than after. [Contact Stephen P. Pryor, CPA](/contact) to talk through whether your specific projects qualify and what the timing looks like given the current bonus depreciation schedule.
